name: Babylonians Begin Visualizing Mathematics
desc: Babylonians are first to understand applied geometry, using triangles to parcel farmland and track celestial bodies. The Greeks would build upon these concepts with roots in logic and eventually Euclid’s Elements.

name: Oldest Evidence of Basket Weaving
desc: Oldest known evidence of basket weaving dates back to c. 24,000 BCE. Impressions of weaving on fired clay found in Moravia, Central Europe, predating settled life.

name: Pythagoras Popularizes Geometric Patterns
desc: Pythagoras credited with popularizing geometrical patterns, “the main feature of 1960s computer art.

name: Blombos Cave Drawing
desc: The earliest known drawing made by humans is generative. Ochre cross-hatching found at Blombos Cave in South Africa is the earliest known drawing yet found anywhere.

name: Emergence of Islamic Geometric Art
desc: Islamic geometric patterns, emerged in the 8th century during the Islamic Golden Age, influenced by Greek, Roman and Sasanian Persian mathematics and ornament.

name: Richard of Wallingford Designs the St Albans Astronomical Clock
desc: Englishman Richard of Wallingford designs the St Albans astronomical clock, an early clockwork machine.

name: Hero of Alexandria Invents Automata
desc: Hero of Alexandria, Greek mathematician and engineer, created a number of automata, including the aeolipile, a steam turbine, a fountain, a wind-powered organ and a puppet theater.

name: Hugh Blackburn Describes the Harmonograph
desc: The Harmonograph, commonly agreed to be invented by Hugh Blackburn, is a mechanical apparatus that creates geometric drawings, typically Lissajous-type figures, through the use of pendulums.

name: Al-Khwārizmī’s Writes Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning
desc: The Persian Al-Khwārizmī's Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning introduced zero, the decimal system and Hindu numerals to the Islamic and European world from India.
subjects: concerning the hindu art of reckoning

name: Ramon Llull Designs the “Logic Machine”
desc: Ramón Llull’s logic machine was a device used to generate new knowledge by mechanically combining concepts and ideas.

name: Luca Pacioli publishes “De Divina Proportione”, illustrated by Leonardo da Vinci
desc: Luca Pacioli’s book, illustrated by Leonardo, helped popularize the principles of mathematical proportion and beauty, known as the Golden Ratio, in art and architecture.

name: Albrecht Dürer Creates Engraving Melencolia I
desc: Packed with meaning and symbols, Melencolia I features a depiction of [Dürer’s solid](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DuerersSolid.html) (the eight-faced stone to the left) whose points form the Dürer graph.

name: Blaise Pascal Builds the Pascaline
desc: It was the first mechanical calculator made in quantity, performing addition and subtraction with an automatic carry between digits.

name: Gottfried Leibniz Pioneers Computational Thinking
desc: Leibniz’s Dissertatio de arte combinatoria (“On the Combinatorial Art” 1666) was one of several cornerstone papers he would write throughout his life on concepts such as symbols, binary systems and formal logic.

name: Gottfried Leibniz Builds the Calculating Machine
desc: Also known as the “stepped reckoner,” this was an early mechanical calculator, demonstrated in wooden model form to the Royal Society in 1673, designed to perform all four arithmetic operations.

name: Jonathan Swift publishes Gulliver’s Travels and includes a description of “the Engine”.
desc: In Gulliver’s Travels, “the Engine” is a device that shuffles words into new combinations, essentially serving as a prototype for a mechanical text generator.

name: Johann Philipp Kirnberger’s Musical Dice Game
desc: Known as Musikalisches Würfelspiel (“musical dice game”), this method first published by Johann Philipp Kirnberger was a monumental event in the history of art and chance.

name: Thomas Bayes develops Bayesian Inference
desc: Thomas Bayes developed this statistical framework, published posthumously by Richard Price, allowing for the quantification of uncertainty and the updating of probabilities based on new evidence.

name: Joseph-Marie Jacquard Invents the Jacquard Loom
desc: The Jacquard loom used punch cards to control the weaving of patterns in fabric. It introduced the notion of a program stored outside the machine on punch cards, which would later result in generative weaving and modern computing.

name: Nicéphore Niépce Produces the Earliest Surviving Camera Photograph
desc: ‍Photography’s impact on modern art is well established but its impact on digital and computer art more specifically is less examined yet central to this story. According to Herbert W.

name: Charles Babbage Develops His Analytical Engine
desc: Foundational to the development of cybernetics, this unrealized mechanical computer aimed to use punch cards, inspired by the [Jacquard Loom](https://timeline.lerandom.art/#/joseph-marie-jacquard-invents-the-jacquard-loom), to perform calculations.

name: Ada Lovelace Publishes the First Algorithm Written for a Machine
desc: Computer programming is born, as Ada Lovelace’s 1843 notes on Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine set out a program for computing Bernoulli numbers, making her the first published computer programmer.

name: William Morris Founds Decorative Arts Firm Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co.
desc: The iconic firm was modeled on a craftsman’s workshop and took a pioneering stand against the non-functional role ascribed to art.

name: Édouard Manet’s Work Rejected by Paris Salon
desc: In what some consider to be the birth of Modernism in art, Manet’s Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe was flatly rejected by the Paris Salon for its unconventional style and subject matter.

name: The Salon des Refusés Opens in Paris
desc: The “exhibition of rejects,” a response to the rejection of many artists' works by the official Salon in Paris, begins.
subjects: académie royale de peinture et de sculpture

name: John Venn’s “graphical indication of randomness” Appears in The Logic of Chance
desc: English logician and mathematician John Venn constructed “a very fair graphical indication of randomness,” according to himself in the third edition of his seminal book, The Logic of Chance.

name: James Clerk Maxwell publishes his theoretical analysis of Watt’s governor
desc: James Clerk Maxwell’s “On Governors”, his theoretical analysis of Watt’s governor published in 1867 and 1868, a device used for regulating the speed of steam engines, was a significant contribution to the understanding of feedback control systems.

name: The First Impressionist Exhibition
desc: This epochal event in art history, held in Paris, marked the emergence of the Impressionist movement, which challenged the cultural monopoly of the Paris Salon and paved the way for modern art.

name: Impressionist Movement Named
desc: Critic Louis Leroy gave the Impressionist movement its name when he accused Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise of being merely a sketch or “impression.” This was meant as insult by Leroy as it implied that Monet’s work was not a finished painting.

name: The Second Impressionist Exhibition
desc: The Second Impressionist Exhibition, held in Paris, was important in consolidating the Impressionist movement as a group and distinct style.

name: “Tulip and Rose” by Morris & Co.
desc: Designed by William Morris and woven for Morris & Co. by the Heckmondwike Manufacturing Company, this was the first dateable Morris design for a woven furnishing textile, important for its budding abstraction.

name: The Third to Eighth Impressionist Exhibitions
desc: The subsequent Impressionist Exhibitions began showcasing more distinct, experimental styles before ultimately fracturing.

name: Art Nouveau Is Born
desc: The term “art nouveau” first appeared in the 1880s in the Belgian journal L’Art Moderne to describe the work of Les Vingt.

name: Seurat Kicks of Post-Impressionism with Pointilism
desc: Seurat begins his best-known painting, A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, completed in 1886.
subjects: a sunday afternoon on the island of la grande jatte

name: Founding of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers
desc: The organization would go on to become the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) in 1963.
subjects: institute of electrical and electronics engineers (ieee)

name: Henri Poincaré Publishes Seminal Paper on the Three-Body Problem
desc: Henri Poincaré's work in the late 19th and early 20th century laid the foundation for the modern science of chaos and complexity, which has been critically influential on computer and generative art.

name: Paul Cézanne’s First Solo Exhibition
desc: The exhibition at Ambroise Vollard’s gallery in Paris was significant for establishing Cézanne as a major artist of his time.

name: First exhibition of Fauvism
desc: The shocking exhibition held in Paris at the Salon d’Automne, featured Fauvist work characterized by bold and experimental use of color, including Henri Matisse’s Woman with a Hat.

name: Cézanne Begins His “Mont Sainte-Victoire” Series
desc: Beginning in the 1870s by the “Father of Post-Impressionism,” this series of forty-five watercolor and thirty-six oil paintings would have an outsized impact on art history.

name: Hermann Muthesius Inspired by visit to Great Britain
desc: German architect Hermann Muthesius, posted to London from 1896, was influenced by the Arts and Crafts Movement, including the latest developments in art and architecture.

name: “Les Demoiselles d’Avignon” by Picasso kicks off Cubism
desc: Cubism, one of the most influential movements of the twentieth century and inspired by Cézanne’s use of basic geometric shapes, is born with Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon.

name: “Group IV, The Ten Largest, No. 7, Adulthood” by Hilma af Klint
desc: Monumental works in the history of abstraction, Swedish artist Hilma af Klint created abstract paintings before the term “abstract art” was even coined. Group IV, The Ten Largest, No.
subjects: hilma af klint: paintings for the future
the secret paintings of hilma af klint

name: Hermann Muthesius Founds the Deutscher Werkbund
desc: The Deutscher Werkbund in Munich, a crucially important and influential association, aimed at improving German design and industry in global markets by partnering product manufacturers with design professionals.

name: Manifesto of Futurism Published by Filippo Tommaso Marinetti
desc: Marinetti’s manifesto called for artists to embrace the aesthetic language of technology and industrialization in their practice.

name: Georges Claude Invents the Neon Light
desc: The invention of neon tubing was a major development in the predecessor of electronic art, Lumino-Kinetic Art.

name: Der Blaue Reiter Exhibition
desc: The radical and provocative first exhibition of the Blue Rider Group, founded by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, was a significant development in the abstraction of art.

name: Sonia and Robery Delaunay Develop Orphism
desc: Inspired by the ideas of Cubism and Futurism, Sonia and Robert Delaunay sought with Orphism to create a new kind of abstract art.

name: Henry van de Velde Forms the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts
desc: Deeply influenced by William Morris’s Arts and Crafts philosophy, Belgian architect and designer Henry van de Velde combined the Arts and Crafts School and the Academy of Fine Arts of Weimar to form the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts.
subjects: academy of fine arts of weimar
weimar school of arts and crafts

name: Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 by Marcel Duchamp
desc: Rejected by the Cubists for appearing too Futurist, this proto-Dadaist painting applies a machine aesthetic to the human form, anticipating the dynamism of Kinetic Art that led to electronic art.

name: Malevich Begins Developing Suprematism
desc: One of the key radical movements in modern art, abstraction and digital generative art history, Kazimir Malevich’s use of geometric forms and limited colors in Suprematism has had a profound impact on art history.

name: “3 Standard Stoppages” by Marcel Duchamp
desc: This revolutionary work of 1913 and 1914 remains one of the most famous examples of the use of chance in the history of art.

name: “Bicycle Wheel” by Marcel Duchamp
desc: This pieces stands as a precursor of both kinetic and conceptual art, another monumental work by Duchamp in the history of generative art.

name: “Prismes électriques” by Sonia Delaunay
desc: Inspired by technological and mechanical innovations of the time, this key work of the Orphism movement sought to explore the effects of color and light in abstract art.

name: Tatlin and Rodchenko Found Constructivism
desc: Named by 1921 and led by Vladimir Tatlin and Alexander Rodchenko, Constructivism is arguably the most influential movement of the first half of the 20th c. on digital and generative art.

name: Kazimir Malevich Stages “The Last Exhibition of Futurist Painting 0.10” in Petrograd
desc: A seminal moment in art history, this exhibition showcased Malevich’s Black Square, Dynamic Suprematism and other abstract works that rejected traditional representational art, marking the birth of the Suprematist movement.

name: “Black Square” by Kazimir Malevich
desc: This work of the Russian avant-garde, painted in 1915 though dated 1913 by Malevich, remains one of art history’s cornerstones.

name: Hugo Ball Founds Dadaism
desc: By emphasizing chance, randomness and absurdity in art, Dada stands as a foundational movement in the development of digital generative art.

name: “Composition with Lines” by Piet Mondrian
desc: This Early Modern oil on canvas was completed during Mondrian’s transition from Cubism to Neoplasticism. A. Michael Noll in 1965 would go on to conduct a famous early computer art experiment with Mondrian’s Composition with Lines.

name: Mondrian and van Doesburg Found De Stijl
desc: Founded by Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg originally as a publication, De Stijl means style in Dutch. It is believed that this magazine, De Stijl, was the first time the term “neo-plasticism” was used.

name: “On Growth and Form” Published by D’Arcy Thompson
desc: The book by Scottish mathematical biologist D’Arcy Thompson showed how mathematical transformations could describe a variety of organic forms.

name: Fountain by Marcel Duchamp
desc: Considered by many to be the first conceptual artwork, a key predecessor of digital generative art, this ready-made of a urinal remains one of the most important works in twentieth century art.

name: “Untitled [Squares Arranged according to the Laws of Chance]” by Hans Arp
desc: This piece’s use of chance demonstrates an early example of an artist relinquishing control to challenge traditional art production techniques.
subjects: untitled (squares arranged according to the laws of chance)
untitled [squares arranged according to the laws of chance]

name: Edouard Jeanneret [Le Corbusier] and Amédée Ozenfant form Purism
desc: The publication of Après le Cubisme (After Cubism) began the Purism movement, proposing “a kind of painting in which objects are represented as powerful basic forms stripped of detail.” Purism relates to electronic and digital generative art due to its embrace of technology and a timeless machine aesthetic.

name: Walter Gropius founds Bauhaus
desc: The revolutionary art school aimed to bring art into contact with everyday life, leveling the distinction between fine and applied art.
subjects: weimar school of arts and crafts

name: “LHOOQ” by Marcel Duchamp
desc: Along with Fountain, this Dada classic of a crude comment below the Mona Lisa on which Duchamp drew a mustache and beard, remains a classic example of irreverence towards traditional art.

name: Marcel Duchamp and Man Ray create “Rotary Glass Plates [Precision Optics]”
desc: An early example of Lumino-kinetic art, progenitor of electronic art, this piece consisted of painted glass plates rotating on an electric motor to create optical illusions.

name: First Dadaist Fair Held in Berlin
desc: A pivotal moment in the history of avant-garde art, the First International Dada-Fair showcased Dada’s anti-art and anti-establishment philosophy of absurdity and provocation to the world for the first time.

name: “Obstruction” by Man Ray
desc: Along with Constructivists Rodchenko and Tatlin, Ray pioneered the use of mobiles (this one composed of 63 coat hangers), paving the way for future kinetic art and eventually all electronic art.

name: Bauhaus Weaving Workshop Initiated by Gunta Stölzl
desc: After Gunta Stölzl asked for a class for women to be set up, the weaving workshop was created by the women themselves and taught by Helena Börner.

name: Students Responsible for Teaching Themselves at Bauhau Weaving Workshop
desc: Master of form Georg Muche “swore never to take a thread in his hand: He did not want to be associated with the feminine aura of weaving.” This led to Gunta Stölzl and Benita Otte taking courses at a technical school to teach their fellow classmates the technical aspects of working a loom.

name: “K VII” by László Moholy-Nagy
desc: Characterized by ordered, geometric forms, the work was completed one year before Moholy-Nagy began teaching at the Bauhaus.

name: Rayograph by Man Ray
desc: Rayographs, photographs made by placing objects directly on sensitized paper and exposing them to light reflected Dada’s interest in chance and the nonsensical.

name: Oskar Schlemmer premières 'Triadisches Ballett'
desc: The Constructivist Bauhaus teacher’s most famous work, this avant-garde artistic dance transformed dancers into geometrical shapes. Schlemmer’s aesthetics would go to influence Japanese Jikken Kobo.

name: László Moholy-Nagy Begins Teaching at Bauhaus
desc: Moholy-Nagy remained at the Bauhaus until 1928, where he focused on painting, lithographs, montage, assemblage and photography.

name: “Construction in Enamel” by László Moholy-Nagy
desc: Moholy-Nagy’s piece, which he described over the telephone to a local enamel factory in Weimar, would go on to influence the Japanese Jikken Kobo movement, particularly Katsuhiro Yamaguchi’s “order art.”

name: “Composition 8” by Wassily Kandinsky
desc: While at the Bauhaus, Kandinsky further developed his Constructivist aesthetic by investigating the use of color, form, and composition to convey emotional and spiritual themes.

name: Bauhaus Repositions
desc: Originally conceived of to unify arts and crafts, the Bauhaus under Gropius began pivoting to design for mass production, adopting the slogan “Art into Industry.”

name: First exhibition of Bauhaus, Weimar
desc: This exhibition showcased the interdisciplinary nature of the school, highlighting works of painting, textiles, sculpture, design, architecture and graphics.

name: “Red and Blue Chair” by Gerrit Rietveld
desc: A canonical artefact of art history and one of the most important pieces of furniture ever built, the chair, designed in 1918 and painted about 1923, composed of 13 square-profiled battens, two rectangular panels and two armrests, was stripped of its volume to emphasize functionality.

name: Bauhaus Weaving Workshop Developes New Aesthetic
desc: Gunta Stölzl leads the women in the Bauhaus weaving workshop to alter its aesthetic, emphasizing tapestries based on abstraction and countering the previous Art-Nouveau narrative.

name: Constructivists Publish Their Manifesto in “Lef”
desc: Constructivism’s manifesto espoused the belief that art should directly reflect the modern industrial world: “The material formation of the object is to be substituted for its aesthetic combination.

name: Mavo movement founded in Japan
desc: Led by Tomoyoshi Murayama, this radical Japanese art movement promulgated an interdisciplinary array of performance art, painting, illustration and architecture to communicate anti-establishment messages to the mainstream.

name: André Breton Writes the “Surrealist Manifesto”
desc: One of the most important predecessors of generative art due to its use of chance, Breton called for artists to bypass reason and rationality by accessing their unconscious mind.

name: “Counter Composition V” by Theo van Doesburg
desc: The signature work of van Doesburg features a simple composition of geometric shapes and colors arranged in a dynamic and asymmetrical pattern.

name: “The Isms of Art” by Hans Arp and El Lissitzky
desc: A critical publication by the leaders of the Dadaist and Constructivist movements documenting the turbulent developemtns of the art world in the first quarter of the twentieth century.

name: Bell Labs Founded
desc: One of the most important developments in digital and generative art’s history, Bell Labs would go on to become instrumental in the development of computational art and animation.

name: International Exposition of Modern Industrial and Decorative Arts, Paris
desc: A key event in the fusion of art and industry, the exhibition saw avant-garde ideas from around the globe presented for the first time. It was instrumental to the development of modern design and architecture.
subjects: international exposition of modern industrial and decorative arts

name: The Bauhaus Moves to the Iconic Dessau Campus
desc: Moving from Weimar to Dessau, this Walter Gropius designed building for the Bauhaus was envisioned as a “Gesamtkunstwerk” (comprehensive artwork).

name: Bauhaus Weavers Revolt
desc: Following the move to Dessau, the weaving workshop relocated to a large studio with new looms.

name: Surrealists Experiment with Rules-Based Chance
desc: Based on parlor games, the group began creating “exquisite corpses,” which involved collaborative and random creations based on a set of rules. This technique was a precursor to rules-based systems producing random results.

name: Gunta Stölzl Named Director of Bauhaus Weaving Workshop
desc: Made head of workshop in 1927 and formally Jungmeister in 1928, holding the post until 1931, Stölzl became the first woman to fill a senior position at the Bauhaus due to the wide support of her students.

name: Kazimir Malevich Publishes “The Non-Objective World”
desc: One of the most important theoretical sources in the development of abstract art, the book articulated the principles of Suprematism, which rejected representation in favor of pure abstraction.

name: Max Ernst Develops Pioneering Method of Chance in Painting, Grattage
desc: A fundamental development in the inclusion of chance in abstract art, grattage involves scraping or scratching the surface of a canvas covered with layers of paint, revealing the textures and patterns created by the different layers.

name: Vannevar Bush constructs his Differential Analyser
desc: Mentioned in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog as an important development in the history of cybernetics, the Differential Analyser was an early mechanical computer, invented by the American engineer, used to solve complex mathematical problems.

name: The Bauhaus Opens Workshops to All Students
desc: Under new director Hannes Meyer, women at the Bauhaus are allowed to choose their own workshops and admitted to study architecture.

name: “Highway and Byways” by Paul Klee
desc: Highways and Byways, a painting by the Swiss artist Paul Klee, is significant for its synthesis of Klee’s interests in geometric abstraction and music. Klee uses color to evoke a sense of movement and rhythm.

name: “Arithmetic Composition” by Theo van Doesburg
desc: A work which presages the mathematics-based, geometric compositions of contemporary generative art, van Doesburg’s piece stands as an example of the De Stijl movement’s attempt to create a new visual language based on geometric forms and primary colors.

name: “Light Prop for an Electric Stage” by László Moholy-Nagy
desc: One of the first electrically powered kinetic sculptures, this kinetic light sculpture is an important example of the historical lineage connecting early Lumino-Kinetic Art to Op and Kinetic art, which led to the development of digital art.
subjects: light prop for an electric stage

name: “Composition with Red Blue and Yellow” by Piet Mondrian
desc: An iconic example of Mondrian’s Neo-Plasticism, characterized by simple geometric, rectilinear forms and primary colors, the piece explores asymmetry, pure planes of color and relational opposites.
subjects: composition with red, blue and yellow

name: Concrete Art Coined by Theo van Doesburg
desc: One of the foundational movements in the history generative art, the Dutch artist and architect’s term describes abstract art based on mathematic or scientific principles with an emphasis on planes and color.

name: “Color Structure” by Joaquín Torres-García
desc: The father of South American geometric abstraction’s seminal work. Color Structure was critical to the development of modernist art in Latin America.

name: Gunta Stölzl Departs the Bauhaus
desc: Gunta Stölzl, pioneering weaver and textile artist, left the Bauhaus due to conflicts with its male-dominated administration, her support for left-wing politics and rising anti-semitism in Germany.

name: Nazis Permanently Close the Bauhaus
desc: The Nazis permanently closed Bauhaus due to their opposition to its modernist and internationalist principles, which they saw as incompatible with their vision of a “pure” and traditional German culture.

name: George David Birkhoff Proposes the “Aesthetic Measure”
desc: This important development in the twentieth-century attempt to measure aesthetics described aesthetic effectiveness by its degree of complexity and order.

name: Black Mountain College Opens
desc: Black Mountain College was founded in North Carolina as an experimental liberal arts college with a focus on the arts, including music, visual arts, and creative writing.

name: “Abstract Composition” by Jean Hélion
desc: Vera Molnar saw this piece and was encouraged to create her own abstract, constructivist-inspired art, the computer art pioneer told Hans Ulrich Obrist.

name: “Endless Rhythm” by Robert Delaunay
desc: Endless Rhythm focuses on geometric shapes and contrasting color, indicating Delaunay’s move towards total abstraction.

name: “Head” by Sophie Taeuber-Arp
desc: The pioneering abstract artist’s sculptures of abstract heads are now considered icons of the Dada movement, a vital predecessor to generative art.

name: “Painterly Architectonic” by Liubov Popova
desc: Helping to introduce Cubism and Futurism into Russian art after visits to France and Italy before WWI, this piece is part of a series that demonstrates Popova’s Suprematist style.

name: Joaquín Torres-García Brings Geometric Abstraction to Latin America
desc: After forty years abroad, the Uruguayan-SpanishTorres-García brought the ideas of geometric abstraction to Latin America in order to reconcile his affinity for the movement with the region’s own cultural traditions.

name: The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even (The Green Box) (La Mariée mise à nu par ses célibataires, même [Boîte verte] ) by Marcel Duchamp
desc: A paramount work in the intersection of chance and art, The Green Box consists of ninety-four loose documents that all related to the idea of chance.
subjects: the bride stripped bare by her bachelors, even

name: Alan Turing Describes the Turing Machine
desc: Considered foundational to the development of computer science, Turing’s “automatic machines” were computational devices consisting of readable and writeable tape that could implement computer algorithms.

name: Konrad Zuse Creates the Z1
desc: Zuse would finish the motor-driven, mechanical computer in 1938. The first freely programmable binary computer, the Z1 laid the groundwork for modern computers by using Boolean logic and incorporating program control.

name: Exhibition of Cubism and Abstract Art, MoMA
desc: A groundbreaking event in the history of abstraction and modernism in North America, this exhibition developed the narrative that adventurous artists were rejecting representation due to having grown “bored with painting facts.” The exhibition marked a shift in the global center of the art world from Europe to New York.

name: László Moholy-Nagy founds the Chicago Institute of Design
desc: Originally known as the New Bauhaus in Chicago, the school attracted former staff from the original Bauhaus such as György Kepes.

name: Konrad Zuse Completes the Z3
desc: The world’s first functioning programmable, digital computer, the Z3 paved the way for future advancements in computer science. Zuse built the Z3 in his parents’ Berlin apartment.

name: Abstract Expressionism Begins
desc: The first American avant-garde movement and deeply influenced by the Surrealist focus on tapping into the unconscious, Abstract Expressionism marked a transition from the hard-edged abstraction of the early twentieth century towards a more spontaneous and emotional form of self-expression.

name: Exhibition by 31 Women at Peggy Guggenheim’s The Art of this Century
desc: Juried by Peggy Guggenheim and Marcel Duchamp, the exhibition was one of the first at Guggenheim’s The Art of this Century.

name: Warren S. McCulloch and Walter Pitts publish “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity”
desc: This influential paper holds immense importance in the development of artificial intelligence (AI), showing that neural networks could perform logical operations and suggested that the brain might work like a digital computer.
subjects: a logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity

name: “Language of Vision” by György Kepes
desc: Kepes, an artist, designer and theoretician, analyzes the effect of visual language on the structure of human consciousness.

name: Birth of Art Informel in France
desc: Responding to the horrors of WWII, European artists rejected the artistic traditions of figurative and geometric work in favor of anti-compositional forms and gestural techniques.

name: Three Spheres I by M. C. Escher
desc: A master of celebrating mathematics, especially geometry, by incorporating it into his art, Escher’s work anticipates the use of a computer to visualize mathematics using algorithms.

name: ENIAC Developed
desc: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), unveiled in February 1946, was the prototype from which modern computers evolved. Developed by John Mauchly and J.

name: The Asociación Arte Concreto-Invención (AACI) Founded
desc: Argentine artist Tomás Maldonado and poet Edgar Bayley founded AACI with their 1945 exhibition and manifesto.

name: Grupo Madí Movement
desc: Formed by artists including Gyula Kosice, Carmelo Arden Quin, and Rhod Rothfuss, Madí embraced concrete art and sought to create a new visual language using abstract shapes and colors, considered an important part of the history of Concrete Art in Latin America.

name: Luminous Structures by Gyula Kosice
desc: The earliest attempt to use neon light as the principal material in a sculpture. Neon art was foundational in the development of lumino-kinetic art and, therefore, electronic art.

name: Birth of Early Digital Tools
desc: This year saw three key developments in the technology that would enable computer art. • The first point plotters begin development: Electronics Associates, Inc.

name: Jean-José Marchand and Georges Mathieu coin the term “lyrical abstraction”
desc: A substyle of the European Art Informel, Lyrical Abstraction favored anti-compositional forms and loose gestural techniques.

name: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Established
desc: This non-profit professional membership group was the first association for computing.

name: Cybernetics Is Born
desc: Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics was published the same year as Claude Shannon’s "A Mathematical Theory of Communication.” Max Bense would apply both their works to aesthetics in his pioneering work, Aesthetica (1965), which laid the theoretical foundations of digital and AI art with computer art.
subjects: art in the age of machine learning

name: Claude Shannon Develops Information Theory with “A Mathematical Theory of Communication”
desc: Claude Shannon’s "A Mathematical Theory of Communication” was published the same year as Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics.

name: The Mathematical Basis of the Arts by Joseph Schillinger
desc: This book, influential to later computer artists, promoted the concept that codified mathematical language could generate art when combined with a machine.
subjects: the mathematical basis of the arts

name: CoBrA Formed
desc: Asger Jorn organized CoBrA with Karel Appel, Constant, Corneille, the writer Christian Dotremont and Joseph Noiret; Pierre Alechinsky joined the following year.

name: Jean Dubuffet’s Art Brut
desc: Dubuffet founded the Compagnie de l’Art Brut to promote the study of Art Brut.

name: William Grey Walter Constructs the First Electronic Autonomous Robots
desc: Built across 1948 and 1949, this self-navigating, pathfinding robot was an important development in cybernetics (and robotics), as it could react to external factors and changing conditions like a biological system.

name: Yoru no Kai Founded
desc: “The Night Society” in English, Yoru no Kai, founded by Taro Okamoto and Kiyoteru Hanada, played a preeminent part in forming Japan’s post-war avant-garde.

name: Yomiuri Indépendant Begins
desc: More commonly referred to as Yomiuri Anpan, the annual non-juried exhibition played a crucial role in the birth of Japanese postwar avant-garde art.

name: "Anni Albers: Textiles” Exhibition at Museum of Modern Art
desc: This landmark exhibition was the Museum of Modern Art’s first devoted to the work of a single textile artist. The exhibitions tour over the next four years would establish Albers as one of the most important artists of her day.

name: Composition by Kenneth Martin
desc: This abstract painting in the Tate collection serves as an important example of material (non-digital) generative art. This work marked Martin’s move towards “pure invention” and rules-based work.

name: Ben Laposky Makes the First Oscillons
desc: Ben Laposky produces the first graphics generated by electronic machines, a critical step on the way to the digitization of generative art with proto-computer art. Using an oscilloscope in 1950, Ben F.

name: “Antennae with Red and Blue Dots” by Alexander Calder
desc: This important example of kinetic sculpture, dated c.1953 by Tate, was created using a set of rules (i.e.
subjects: antennae with red and blue dots

name: Alejandro Otero Begins His Collage Work
desc: This major Venezuelan kinetic artist and abstract geometric painter began his collage work with found materials inspired by Mondrian. These would lead to one of his significant contributions, Coloritmo (Colorhythms).

name: Jesús Rafael Soto Settles in Paris
desc: A seminal figure in the development of Kinetic Art, Soto’s arrival in Paris put him in contact with Victor Vasarely, Yaacov Agam, Jean Tinguely and others connected with the Salon des Réalités Nouvelles.

name: John von Neumann Devises Cellular Automata
desc: The Hungarian-American mathematician von Neumann’s conception of cellular automata (CA), suggested by Stanislaw Ulam, demonstrated the potential for simple rules to give rise to complex and unpredictable behavior.

name: Ivan Moscovich Begins Experimenting with Mathematical Forms
desc: Mathematician Ivan Moscovich experimented with different mechanisms to create complex curves and shapes based on mathematical formulas.

name: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds Build the SNARC Neural Network Machine
desc: SNARC (Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator), the first artificial neural network, was composed of simple electronic circuits that could learn from their environment and adjust their behavior accordingly.

name: The Ferranti Mark I Is the First Commercially Available Electronic Computer
desc: Based on its prototype, the legendary Manchester Mark I, the Ferranti Mark I was the world’s first commercially available general-purpose digital computer.

name: Jikken Kobo Begins
desc: Meaning “Experimental Workshop” in English, Jikken Kobo was a radically experimental Japanese art collective, with a highly Deleuzian approach to art and the technology of the time.

name: Gutai Movement in Japan
desc: Founded by Jiro Yoshihara, Gutai was a radically experimental movement even by today’s standards.

name: Hiroshi Kawano Publishes His First Algorithmic Images
desc: Kawano, an information aesthetics scholar and one of the earliest pioneers in using computer algorithms to create artistic compositions, placed the computer at the center of artistic generation.

name: CTG Pioneers Digital Generative Systems
desc: Computer Technique Group, a Tokyo-based student collective, was founded in 1966.

name: Yoichiro Kawaguchi Develops the GROWTH Model
desc: One of this story’s greatest legends. Kawaguchi will go on to win the 2010 ACM SIGGRAPH Distinguished Artist Award for Lifetime Achievement. But his creative career began around this time in the late ‘70s.

name: Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM) in Japan
desc: Defined by the pursuit of new artistic expression that incorporates technology and media, the Center continues to play an important role in showcasing, cultivating and supporting the generative art community in Japan.
subjects: yamaguchi center for arts and media (ycam)

name: Imaginary・Numbers by Keiko Kimoto
desc: This award-winning installation generates an infinite series of abstract images based on mathematical formulas and random elements.

name: Generativemasks by Takawo
desc: Honed over the course of several years through Takawo’s “dailycoding” practice beginning in 2015, Generativemasks features symmetrical geometric patterns that speak to generative art’s lush digital and material history.

name: Victor Vasarely’s Yellow Manifesto Lays Generative Art’s Conceptual Foundation
desc: Victor Vasarely’s seminal Yellow Manifesto envisioned a synthesis between art and technology to enhance art’s accessibility through mass production.

name: Computer-Generated Pictures, Howard Wise Gallery
desc: On display in April 1965, the legendary Computer-Generated Pictures introduced computer art to the broader public, especially in the United States.
subjects: ninety parallel sinusoids with linearly increasing period

name: “Cybernetic Serendipity” Defines a Movement
desc: Cybernetic Serendipity, Jasia Reichardt’s landmark international exhibition at the Institute of Contemporary Arts, London, ran from 2 August to 20 October 1968 and was computer art’s first international exhibition.
subjects: art in the age of machine learning

name: Harold Cohen Pioneers AI Art with AARON
desc: AARON, the autonomous drawing machine Cohen named at Stanford in 1973, pioneered the use of AI to create art.

name: Casey Reas and Ben Fry Initiate Processing Project
desc: Perhaps important enough for the name of the entire decade, Processing is that important to the development of generative art.

name: Jennifer and Kevin McCoy’s Quantum
desc: NFTs Enable Digital Ownership While previous explorations of the blockchain existed prior to Jennifer and Kevin McCoy’s Quantum—many of them can be found previously on this Timeline—none presented a complete package of what NFTs would be than the McCoys.

name: “Imaginary Landscape No 4″ by John Cage
desc: The singular pioneer of generative music, John Cage began to utilize chance in his compositions around this time with “Imaginary Landscape No 4″ and “Music of Changes.” In “Imaginary Landscapes,” twelve radios were played at once with their broadcasts determined by chance and out of Cage’s control.

name: Spectrum Colors Arranged by Chance by Ellsworth Kelly
desc: Composed during his time in France, this part of a series of chance-arranged spectrum collages marked the shift of Kelly’s work towards chance methodologies as well as work on a grid.

name: “Electronic Abstractions” by Ben Laposky
desc: The Origins of Computer Art This series of experimental artworks by Ben Laposky was generated on analogue equipment by photographing oscilloscope patterns created by electronic circuits.

name: “Abstronic” by Mary Ellen Bute
desc: Pioneering work of abstract electronic animation Using an oscilloscope, Bute was the creator of some of the earliest electronically generated images.

name: Birth of Neo-Dada
desc: While not formally named until the early 1960s by Barbara Rose, we consider the birth of Neo-Dada to have occurred in 1952 with John Cage’s Theater Piece No. 1.

name: “Theater Piece No. 1” by John Cage
desc: Kicking off the Neo-Dada movement and critical to the development of performance art, Cage’s Theater Piece No. 1 paved the way for the movement’s collaborative, multimedia and chance-based nature.

name: “Suite for Five” by Merce Cunningham
desc: A hugely important moment in Chance Dance and with a score by John Cage, Suite for Five is a Neo-Dada classic.

name: “Love-Letters” by Christopher Strachey
desc: A landmark in the history of computer-generated text, Strachey’s love letter algorithm (or M.U.C.) created generative poems by combining words selected from a database via the random generator of the Ferranti Mark I.

name: Founding of the Independent Group (IG)
desc: The Independent Group (IG), a collective of British artists, critics, and designers who came together in the early 1950s, explored the intersection of pop culture, mass media imagery, and art in technology.

name: “Mood Contrasts” by Mary Ellen Bute
desc: Bute’s oscillograph-made, pioneering abstract film saw Rimsky Korsakov’s “Hymn to the Sun” and “Dance of the Tumblers” visually interpreted by an array of Surrealist visual images.

name: Oscillons 34, 26, 14, 47 by Ben Laposky
desc: These pivotal works of proto-computer art serve as a link between analog and the upcoming digital art-making devices.

name: “Plans mobiles” by Pol Bury
desc: Plans mobiles (Mobile Planes), made from 1953 to 1955, perfectly illustrates a “new energy from the possibility of movement” in art.

name: Jikken Kōbō’s Fifth Presentation Introduces the Autoslide Works
desc: As proto-video art, this exhibition was an important precursor to electronic art. It combined experimentally composed music with surrealistic visuals.

name: Max Bense Begins Publishing Aesthetica
desc: Bense’s Aesthetica, foundational to computer art history, established the theoretical foundation of computer art.

name: Ivan Serpa Founds The Grupo Frente
desc: The Brazilian movement rejected strict adherence to the orthodoxy of purity, science, and math. Grupo Frente was interested in representing organic, nonfigurative forms.

name: Whirlwind and SAGE Initiatives by US Military Funding Spark Computing Innovations
desc: In 1954, Douglas Ross created the “Scope Input Program.” This program made for Whirlwind computers was the first example of hand-drawing with a computer.

name: The Term “Artificial Intelligence” Is Coined
desc: John McCarthy coined the term “artificial intelligence” in a proposal for a Dartmouth College study written with Marvin Minsky (Harvard University), Nathaniel Rochester (IBM) and Claude Shannon (Bell Telephone Laboratories).

name: “Le Mouvement” Is First Post-War Kinetic Exhibition
desc: The April 1955 exhibition at the Galerie Denise René, in which Vasarely was central, launched both Op and Kinetic Art, while inspiring the New Tendencies group GRAV. It’s thus a pivotal moment in the history of generative art.

name: “Experimental Outdoor Exhibition of Modern Art to Challenge the Midsummer Sun” by Gutai
desc: This legendary outdoor exhibition featured radical concepts that were a decade ahead of their time.
subjects: experimental outdoor exhibition of modern art to challenge the midsummer sun

name: Ben Laposky Releases Colored Electronic Image
desc: In a follow up Electronic Abstractions, Laposky released a colored version of his electronic images, Oscillons. These early colored analogue graphics were created with an oscilloscope by manipulating electronic waves.

name: Herbert W. Franke Begins Creating Art with an Oscillograph
desc: Franke’s Pendular Oscillogram, made with a cathode ray oscillograph built by his friend Dr Franz Raimann, is considered, along with Laposky’s Electronic Abstraction, to be one of the first pieces of (analog) computer art.

name: CYSP 1 by Nicolas Schöffer
desc: This mobile kinetic sculpture is considered the first cybernetic sculpture.

name: “The New Landscape in Art and Science” by György Kepes
desc: A precursor to C. P. Snow’s “two cultures” thesis of 1959, The New Landscape in Art and Science was a book that attempted to combat the growing pessimism in the art world towards the mixing of art and science.
subjects: the new landscape in art and science

name: 2nd Gutai Outdoor Exhibition in Ashiya Park
desc: Following the first exhibition, the group continued to enhance audience participation. It even anticipated the communal drawing practices of the net art community.

name: “Electric Dress” by Atsuko Tanaka
desc: The Gutai member’s best known work was constructed by fashioning vividly painted light bulbs into a dress. The piece consists of only light bulbs and their cords.

name: John Backus Releases FORTRAN
desc: Conceived in 1954, the programming language of early computer art, Fortran (FORMula TRANslator) is one of the oldest high-level programming languages.

name: “An Experiment in Musical Composition” is Published
desc: This consequential paper by Brooks, Hopkins, Neumann and Wright outlines how a computer can be used as a system to create art.

name: “Syntactic Structures” by Noam Chomsky
desc: Chomsky’s epochal book influenced both mid-century computational theory and artificial intelligence by introducing the concept of Transformational-Generative Grammar, “the most significant development in linguistic theory and research in the 20th century.” Generative Grammar seeks to explain how humans are able to produce and understand an infinite number of grammatically correct sentences.

name: ZERO Forms in Düsseldorf
desc: Founded by Otto Piene and Heinz Mack in Düsseldorf, four years before New Tendencies, Zero was inspired by the notion of starting over (hence the name).

name: Black Mountain College Closes
desc: The spiritual successor to the Bauhau closed after 24 years primarily due to financial difficulties. It had been opened in 1933 by John A. Rice, who hired the Bauhaus’s Josef Albers.

name: Richard Hamilton Lists the ‘Characteristics of Pop Art’
desc: According to Hamilton, an early progenitor of Pop Art: “Pop Art is: Popular (designed for a mass audience), Transient (short-term solution), Expendable (easily forgotten), Low cost, Mass produced, Young (aimed at youth), Witty, Sexy, Gimmicky, Glamorous, Big business” Similar words have been used to derisively describe the on-chain art of today.

name: Allan Kaprow Begins Making ‘Environments’
desc: Environments, precursors to “happenings” as well as the Performance and Installation Art of the ‘60s-‘70s, were large-scale, immersive installations intended to engage all of the senses of the viewer.

name: Duchamp Gives His Famous Talk, “The Creative Act”
desc: In this talk, Duchamp explained the importance of chance in the creative act.

name: Max Mathews Develops MUSIC I
desc: Mathews, computer music pioneer, developed the computer music composition language on an IBM 704 while at Bell Labs. MUSIC I was the first demonstration of computer synthesized music.

name: A. P. Rich Writes Program for the Design of Wave Patterns for Textiles
desc: Rich, of the Applied Physics Laboratory, Johns Hopkins University, wrote one of the earliest examples of using a computer program for graphic design, according to Herbert W. Franke. This was of wave patterns for textiles.

name: “Theorie de l’information et perception esthetique (Information Theory and Esthetic Perception)” by Abraham A. Moles
desc: Information Theory and Esthetic Perception by Abraham A. Moles, later professor at Strasbourg University, was an early, important work on information aesthetics. Moles combined Shannon’s information theory with aesthetics.
subjects: théorie de l'information et perception esthétique

name: Voyage II, Frank Malina
desc: This piece by Malina, pioneer of Lumino-Kinetic art, demonstrates the development of the Lumino-Kinetic movement towards electronic art.

name: “Fontana Mix”, John Cage
desc: This landmark, hugely influence piece of chance music consists of a graphic score of transparent sheets the performer superimposes to derive a realisation.

name: “Méta-matic No. 8” by Jean Tinguely
desc: Foreshadowing the plotter, the Swiss kinetic sculptor’s key piece in the history of chance in art, Méta-matic No. 8, was an animated sculpture made from found material.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Minimalism Emerges with “16 Americans” at MoMA
desc: A rebuke of gestural art and extension of modern art’s abstraction, Minimalism emerged in the late ‘50s with exhibitions such as Frank Stella’s Black Paintings at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

name: Béla Julesz Invents Random-dot Stereograms
desc: Julesz’s “Two Image Random Dot Stereograms” were 2 side-by-side randomly generated dot images. When viewed through a stereoscope they created the sensation of depth.

name: Raymond Scott Builds the Electronium, an Instrument for Generative Composition
desc: Scott developed this important proto-digital generative art (in this case music) with his Electronium. This device was an early synthesizer combined with algorithmic compositions which produced generative music.

name: Herbert W. Franke’s “Experimentelle Ästhetik” Exhibition
desc: The exhibition was held at the Museum of Applied Arts in Vienna, presenting the experimental images of the then physicist-artist, Herbert W. Franke.

name: CalComp 565 Drum Plotter Released
desc: One of the earliest computer graphics output devices sold and the first drum plotter printer, the CalComp 565 could produce large-scale drawings with precise lines, becoming a popular tool for computer artists.

name: Gustav Metzger Begins Creating “Auto-Destructive Art”
desc: To protest nuclear war and showcase his values of spontaneity and randomness, Metzger creates his first acid paintings. This form of material generative art is created by spraying acid onto sheets of nylon.

name: “The Two Cultures” Lecture by C.P. Snow
desc: C.P. Snow’s “Two Cultures” lecture was a call to bridge the divide between the sciences and the humanities, embodied by the multi-disciplinary computer art.

name: “18 Happenings in 6 Parts” by Allan Kaprow
desc: Kaprow’s seminal exhibition was the first Happenings and coined the term as art form. Happenings were avant-garde, interactive art events that paved the way for Performance Art and Fluxus.

name: “Manifesto Neoconcreto” by Ferreira Gullar
desc: Gullar’s manifesto advocated for a new kind of art that rejected the formalism of traditional concrete art and embraced a more humanistic, participatory approach.

name: Theo Lutz produces “Stochastic Texts”
desc: This key development in the pre-history of computer-generated literature was an early use of a computer to generate text. Lutz’s “stochastic texts” were produced at Stuttgart when Max Bense was there developing Aesthetica.

name: Tête barbue (Bearded Head) by Jean Dubuffet
desc: This important example in the history of chance in art consists of simply a found piece of driftwood that happened to look like something else.

name: William Fetter Creates the First Computer Graphics
desc: At the Wichita Branch of the Military Aircraft Systems Division of Boeing, William Fetter coined the term “computer graphics” to refer to his plotter drawings.

name: Karl Otto Götz Manually Anticipates Digital Generative Art
desc: Karl Götz’s Statistisch-metrische Modulation (Statistical-metrical Modulation) is a series of hand-drawn Raster Pictures of 2 x 2 cm black and white squares on pieces of variously-sized cardboard.

name: John Whitney Sr. Founds “Motion Graphics Incorporated”
desc: John Whitney Sr., pioneer in the field of computer-generated art and animation, founded Motion Graphics Incorporated. It became one of the first companies to use computers for creating graphics and animation.

name: Vera Molnar Co-Founds Centre de Recherche d’Art Visuel, (later Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV))
desc: Playing a significant role in the development of Kinetic and Op Art, the Parisian collective aimed to explore the relationship between art, science and technology to create works that empirically engaged with new materials and challenged traditional notions of art.

name: “Automat und Mensch Kybernetische Tatsachen und Hypothesen” by Karl Steinbuch
desc: Steinbuch’s books introduced the concept of “information processing” as a core function of machines and computers. This idea laid the foundation for the development of artificial intelligence and cognitive science.
subjects: automat und mensch: a history of ai and generative art

name: Henry Flynt Coins “Concept Art”
desc: “’Concept art’ is first of all an art of which the material is ‘concepts.’” -Henry Flynt in “Concept Art” Flynt, an American philosopher, musician and artist, coined the term “concept art” in his 1961 essay “Concept Art”, published in An Anthology in 1963.

name: George Maciunas’s “Bread & AG” Opens in New York, the First Fluxus Event
desc: The Lithuanian-American artist and curator, Maciunas founded and organized the Fluxus (“flowing” in English) movement’s first event.

name: “Nove tendencije” the first New Tendencies exhibition opens at the Gallery for Contemporary Art, Zagreb
desc: Dissatisfied with 1960 Venice Biennale, Brazilian artist Almir Mavignier and art critic Matko Meštrović sought to organize a new exhibition that showcased “new tendencies” in art not yet supported by the establishment.

name: Invention of the Zuse Graphomat Z 64
desc: Presented for the first time at the Hanover Fair, this revolutionary drawing machine would be used by early computer pioneers such as Georg Nees and Frieder Nake.

name: “Symbols, Signals, and Noise” by John R. Pierce
desc: This book played an important role in the development of cybernetic theory, stating that “art was clearly a communication phenomenon,” according to Grant Taylor.
subjects: théorie de l'information et perception esthétique

name: “An Approach to Cybernetics” by Gordon Pask
desc: An Approach to Cybernetics by Gordon Pask is a foundational text in the field of cybernetics, which explores the principles of information and control in complex systems.

name: “Variations luminodynamiques” by Nicolas Schöffer
desc: The founder of Cybernetic Art, Schöffer’s pioneering work of video art was an experimental program broadcast on French Television. The Surrealistic 9 min and 10 second film is in the permanent collection of the Centre Pompidou.

name: “Epidauros II” by Barbara Hepworth
desc: This giant of modernist sculpture, Hepworth’s Epidauros II and its “pure form” would influence Roman Verostko’s work at that time and throughout his career.

name: “The Responsive Eye”, MoMA
desc: The exhibition by William C. Seitz at The Museum of Modern Art ignited Opto-Kinetic Art and even inspired Vera Molnár shortly after.

name: “Dragons Emerging from the Forest” by Kazuo Shiraga
desc: This work by a key member of the Japanese Gutai movement serves as an example of their groundbreaking use of chance. Shiraga swung, slipped and spun back and forth from a rope attached to the ceiling with wet oil paint on his feet.

name: “Grand tir–séance Galerie J” by Niki de Saint Phalle
desc: This convention-defying work of chance art saw Saint Phalle create an assemblage of white, found objects, surrounded by sacks of colored paint. She would then fire a rifle at the paint sacks to explosively create the work.

name: A. Michael Noll Creates some of the First Creative Graphics with a Digital Computer; Terms Phrase “Programmer-Artist”
desc: The First Computer Art Experimenting on the side with computer-generated creative expression while at Bell Labs, Noll avoided calling the works he documented and produced “art.” He referred to them instead as “patterns” in order to avoid controversy.

name: The US Company (USCO) Garners Interest for Science and Technology in Art
desc: This group, which formed in 1962, played a critical role in expanding interest in science and technology in art in the United States. The group toured widely with multimedia performances, championing technology in art.

name: Umberto Eco Coins “Programmed Art”
desc: Eco used the term “programmed art” for the Italian kinetic works shown at Olivetti by Gruppo T, Gruppo N, Enzo Mari and Bruno Munari. Programmed art extended the aesthetics and concepts of Constructivism and Neo-Plasticism.

name: American Pop Art Bursts onto the Scene
desc: With no prior personal relationships and independently from one another, American Pop Art exploded in 1962 with four monumental exhibitions.

name: “Augmenting Human Intellect” by Douglas Engelbart
desc: In this seminal report for the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Engelbart proposed the idea of using technology to enhance human cognitive abilities.
subjects: air force office of scientific research

name: “The Open Work” by Umberto Eco
desc: The Open Work, a book by Umberto Eco, proposed the idea of art as a process of interaction between the artwork and the viewer, rather than a fixed object.

name: “Music from Mathematics”, the First Computer Music Issued on Record
desc: The first commercially issued recording of computer generated music, Music from Mathematics ([full album](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Ep6kXOha0U&t=1s&ab_channel=alexdinunzio)), created by John R.

name: “The Great Experiment: Russian Art, 1863-1922” by Camilla Gray
desc: The first English-language book about the Russian avant-garde covers the Constructivist and Suprematist movements of the early twentieth-century.

name: Lee Harrison III Builds ANIMAC
desc: ANIMAC, a hybrid graphic animator and precursor to Scanimate was an early motion capture system. It featured sensors mounted on a person that were captured on a screen.

name: Clark and Molnar Invent the LINC
desc: Considered the first individual computer work station, the LINC (Laboratory INstrument Computer) was an important forerunner of the personal computer developed by Wes Clark and Charles Molnar at the MIT Lincoln Laboratory.

name: Ivan Sutherland Invents “Sketchpad”
desc: One of the first graphical user interfaces, Sketchpad was the first interactive computer graphics programs.

name: Military Agencies Create Early Computer-Generated Art
desc: These objects are some of the first creative computer-generated imagery along with A. Michael Noll’s Patterns by 7090 from a year earlier in 1962.
subjects: united states army ballistic research laboratories

name: “Computers and Automation” Births “Computer Art”
desc: “Computer art” is born! The trade journal Computers and Automation significantly impacted the infancy of computer art.

name: “9 Evenings: Theatre and Engineering” at the 69th Regiment Armory
desc: The event that legitimized the use of technology in art, Artist Robert Rauschenberg and engineer Billy Klüver (Bell Labs) organized 9 Evenings to promote artist-engineer collaboration.

name: “Condensation Cube” by Hans Haacke
desc: Condensation Cube (1963–65) is a sealed transparent acrylic cube containing a small quantity of water.

name: “Gaussian Quadratic” by A. Michael Noll
desc: One of the most iconic works of early computer art, Noll’s Gaussian Quadratic is a computer-generated artwork consisting of a series of connected lines generated by mathematical algorithms, Noll created while working at Bell Labs.

name: “compArt ER 56 series” and “Random Polygon Move” Signal Frieder Nake’s Entrance into Computer Art
desc: 1963 marks the year that Nake, the computer art pioneer, began making computer art. His compArt ER56 series refers to the program created to produce his work from 1963 to 1965.

name: Doug Engelbart Designs the First Computer Mouse
desc: Doug Engelbart, a computer engineer, conceived the first computer mouse, which his engineer Bill English built from wood with one button.

name: “Exposition of Music—Electronic Television” Exhibition by Nam June Paik
desc: Paik’s first exhibit, at Galerie Parnass in Wuppertal in March 1963, marked the birth of video art and represented turning point in the dematerialization of art.

name: “Simulation of a Two-Gyro Gravity-Gradient Attitude Control System” by Edward E. Zajac
desc: Constructed by Zajac at Bell Labs, this is frequently credited as the first computer animation.

name: ASCII Adopted as Standard
desc: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) was adopted as a standard in 1963. This code is a character encoding system that assigns unique numbers to represent each letter and character of the alphabet.

name: “Inventing the Future” by Dennis Gabor
desc: In his book Inventing the Future, Gabor discusses the role of science and technology in shaping the future of society.

name: Galanter Defines Generative Art
desc: In his seminal text from over twenty years ago, Galanter asks and answers, “What is Generative Art?” in the must-read essay for anyone interested in generative art: [“What is Generative Art?

name: Edmund C. Berkeley Begins Publishing “Computers and Automation”
desc: Beginning in September 1951, Edmund C. Berkeley published Computers and Automation, the first magazine dedicated to the computing revolution.

name: The First Man (Boeing Man) by William Fetter
desc: At Boeing in Seattle, where Fetter moved in 1963, he and his team were the first to draw a human figure using a computer.

name: Roy Ascott’s First Show: “Diagram-boxes and Analogue Structures”
desc: Ascott, British cybernetic and telematics arts pioneer, had his first exhibition at the Molton Gallery, London, in February 1963 with Diagram-boxes and Analogue Structures.

name: First Piece of Computer Art Criticism by Arnold Rockman and Leslie Mezei
desc: Arnold Rockman, art critic, and Leslie Mezei, computer scientist, together wrote: “the first recognizable piece of computer art criticism.
subjects: the electronic computer as an artist

name: US Army’s BRL Wins Computer Art Content Top Prize for Second Straight Year
desc: The United States Army Ballistic Research Laboratories won the Computers and Automation “Computer Art Contest” first prize for the second straight year with Trajectories of a Ricocheting Projectile.
subjects: united states army ballistic research laboratories

name: Leslie Mezei Gives the First Lecture on Computer Art
desc: Canadian Leslie Mezei, computer art pioneer and scholar, played a hugely important and influential role in the development of computer graphics.
subjects: computing and data processing society of canada

name: “’monument’ for V. Tatlin” by Dan Flavin
desc: The first of Flavin’s homages to Vladimir Tatlin, co-founder of Constructivism, alludes to the Constructivist focus on modest industrial materials.

name: Time Popularizes “Op Art”
desc: Despite Victor Vasarely spawning the movement nearly a decade earlier with the manifesto and subsequent exhibition, Le Mouvement, the term “Op Art” was popularized in 1964 by Time Magazine, though its coinage is contested.

name: “23-Ecke” by Georg Nees
desc: 23-Ecke (Polygon of 23 Vertices) is believed to be the pioneer Nees’s first work. It was shown the following year at Computergrafik, the first ever computer art exhibition, organised by Max Bense in Stuttgart.

name: “Five Screens with Computer” by Gustav Metzger
desc: Hearing the words “five screens with computer” today, our minds automatically think of a laptop or desktop computer’s “screen” or digital display.

name: “The machine, as seen at the end of the mechanical age” at MoMA
desc: The iconic exhibition inspired Software and facilitated art’s transition from the mechanical to the digital. Curated by collector and museum director, K.G.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Software at the Jewish Museum, New York
desc: Software - Information Technology: Its New Meaning for Art showcased programmed art’s potential as a creative tool. The experimental exhibition was curated by Jack Burnham.

name: “Pour une peinture expérimentale programmée,” in Groupe de recherche d’art visuel (Paris: Galerie Denise René; GRAV)
desc: In the catalogue for this early GRAV exhibition, Morellet would spell out the group’s relevance to the programmed, digital generative art of today.

name: The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society Holds its First Annual Exhibition
desc: These annual exhibitions by the newly formed Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society aimed to raise the cultural standing and awareness of craft work, such as ceramics, textiles, metalwork and furniture.

name: “Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society” Officially Gives Arts & Crafts Movement its Name
desc: Founded in London and born out of the influence of William Morris and Philip Webb, the society’s objective was “to assert a new public relevance for the work of decorative artists.” Arts & Crafts sought to erase the distinction between fine art, design and craft, while uniting creativity and manufacturing.
subjects: weimar school of arts and crafts

name: “Systemic Painting” Exhibition, The Guggenheim Museum
desc: This systems-based art exhibit would enable future digital generative practices. Curated by critic Lawrence Alloway, the exhibition coined the phrase “systemic painting” for systems-based work.

name: The World’s First Computer Art Exhibition: “Georg Nees: Computergrafik”, Studiengalerie der TH Stuttgart
desc: Opening 4 February and running from the 5th to the 19th, Computergrafik was the first of the three 1965 computer art exhibitions globally.

name: “Thinking Machines: Art and Design in the Computer Age, 1959–1989” at MoMA
desc: The exhibition, along with Open Codes at ZKM, indicated renewed institutional interest in computer-generated art prior to the impact of NFTs.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age
thinking machines: art and design in the computer age, 1959–1989

name: Kenneth C. Knowlton develops BEFLIX
desc: Knowlton, a pioneer of computer art and animation, at Bell Labs developed BEFLIX, the first general-purpose programming language for computer animation.

name: First version of BASIC Released
desc: John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz released version 1 of the programming language, BASIC (Beginner’s All-Purpose Symbolic Instruction Code).

name: Marshall McLuhan Published Book "Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man”
desc: The book that coined the phrase “the medium is the message,” Understand Media is a significant work in media theory and art history.
subjects: understanding media: the extensions of man

name: The Foundational “Aesthetica” Published by Max Bense is Finished
desc: This 348-page tome by Max Bense, Aesthetica. Einführung in die neue Aesthetik, contained four volumes and a manifesto. Bense published the four volumes between 1954 and 1960; the 1965 edition collects them and adds the manifesto.
subjects: art in the age of machine learning

name: 13/9/65 Nr. 2 (“Hommage à Paul Klee”) by Frieder Nake
desc: One of the most cited and recognized works among the earliest computer art, Homage to Paul Klee (in English) draws inspiration from Klee’s Hauptweg und Nebenwege (1929) without Nake directly attempting to reproduce it algorithmically.

name: “Schotter” by Georg Nees
desc: This iconic early computer-generated drawing features squares on a grid that become increasingly disordered from top to bottom, exploring what would become a central theme in computer generative art, the relationship between order and disorder.

name: “Computer Composition with Lines” by A. Michael Noll
desc: One of the computer art pioneer’s legendary pieces, Computer Composition with Lines won Computer and Automation’s first prize in 1965.

name: “Portrait of the Machine As a Young Artist” by John R. Pierce in Playboy One of the Earliest Computer Art Essays
desc: This landmark essay in the popular magazine for men helped nudge computer art into mainstream culture. Written by Bell Labs’s John R. Pierce, the title refers to the James Joyce novel, alluding to the computer as a maturing artist.
subjects: portrait of the machine as a young artist

name: “Electronic Art" Exhibition by Nam June Paik at Galeria Bonino (New York)
desc: This early Paik exhibit sought to establish the television as an artistic medium. Along with another of his exhibitions at Bonino (1968), these would establish the artist as a pioneer of video art.

name: “Four Self-Distorting Grids” by François Morellet
desc: Exemplifying the influence of Kinetic Art on Op art, this motorized, kinetic structure demonstrates that Op Art did not have to solely rely on virtual movement.

name: “Four-Dimensional Hyperobjects” by A. Michael Noll
desc: Made by Noll at Bell Labs, this stereoscopic film of a “hypercube” is one of the earliest 3D computer graphic films. Images were printed side-by-side, frame-by-frame and are meant for 3D freeviewing (like a “Magic Eye”).

name: nul 1965, Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam
desc: As Gutai gained fame in Europe, Jiro Yoshihara, accompanied by his son Michio, was invited to exhibit in Amsterdam. Only three-dimensional and new works were allowed with no paintings.

name: “Computer-Produced Movies” by Kenneth C. Knowlton
desc: The article in which Knowlton explains BEFLIX and his early computer animation techniques, which he developed at Bell Labs.

name: Maughan S. Mason’s Traveling Show of Analog Computer Generated Works
desc: Arranged by the Western Association of Art Museums, the show featured Mason’s analog computer work, much of it would later be included in Cybernetic Serendipity.

name: “Information Theory and Esthetic Perception” by Abraham Moles
desc: First published in French in 1958, and drawing from Claude Shannon’s Information Theory as well as George David Birkhoff, Moles aimed to use techniques of information theory to analyze art.
subjects: théorie de l'information et perception esthétique

name: “Composition with Squares” and "Walk-through-Raster” by Frieder Nake
desc: Nake won the first prize of the 1966 Computers and Automation contest with an untitled drawing of small squares, recorded by Compart as Zufällige Zeichenverteilung (1965).

name: Sol LeWitt Begins Producing “Serial” Work
desc: LeWitt’s Serials marked the beginning of his important rules-based, systems work that could produce many possible outcomes.

name: “Primary Structures” Exhibition at The Jewish Museum Helps Introduce Minimalism
desc: The exhibition was the first in the United States to showcase the emerging Minimalism movement, presenting simplified geometric sculptures made with colorful, industrial materials.

name: E.A.T. Holds Its Press Launch at Rauschenberg’s Studio
desc: Following its first meeting in November 1966, EAT held its press launch at co-founder Robert Rauschenberg’s Manhattan studio. The meeting was attended by a variety of artists and engineers (from IBM and Bell Labs).

name: “Kunst-Licht-Kunst” Artificial Light Exhibition
desc: According to Art Historian Frank Popper, this exhibition was “one of the founding moments of technological art.” Featuring work from Man Ray, László Moholy-Nagy and others, the exhibition showcased the use of light in contemporary art and sculpture.

name: “Interference” by Jean-Pierre Yvaral
desc: The work by Victor Vasarely’s son, part of a series, was made of cord, steel and wood to create the illusion of pulsation and dynamism.

name: “Untitled (one gallon of industrial high-gloss enamel, poured)” by William Anastasi
desc: This piece stands as an important example of chance in art as well as an early conceptual and material generative art piece.
subjects: untitled (one gallon of industrial high-gloss enamel, poured)

name: "Behaviourist Art and the Cybernetic Vision” by Roy Ascott
desc: Artist Roy Ascott elucidated his detailed theory of cybernetic art in a two-part article for the journal Cybernetica, published in 1966 and 1967.
subjects: behaviourist art and the cybernetic vision

name: “Herstellung von zeichnerischen Darstellungen, Tonfolgen und Texten mit elektronischen Rechenanlagen” (Production of graphic renderings, audio sequences, and texts by electronic computers) Exhibition
desc: This exhibition at the Deutsche Rechenzentrum (German Computing Center) in Darmstadt featured computer music, drawings and text. It helped to popularize computer art in Germany and beyond.

name: Teletype Corporation develops Inktronic
desc: Printing 1,200 words per minute, this was one of the earliest inkjet printers, known as a teleprinter.

name: Experiments in Art and Technology Founded with “EAT News”
desc: Founded by engineers Billy Klüver and Fred Waldhauer and artists Robert Rauschenberg and Robert Whitman, following the success of their 9 Evenings show, the aim of Experiments in Art and Technology (EAT) was to promote collaboration between engineers and artists.

name: Sol LeWitt Defines Conceptual Art in Print
desc: In his [essay](https://monoskop.org/images/3/3d/LeWitt_Sol_1967_1999_Paragraphs_on_Conceptual_Art.pdf) “Paragraphs on Conceptual Art,” LeWitt fixed the term in art-world usage, famously writing that “the idea becomes a machine that makes the art.” LeWitt continued: “I will refer to the kind of art in which I am involved as conceptual art.

name: Charles Csuri Enters the Computer Art Scene with Series of Important Works
desc: Charles “Chuck” Csuri exploded onto the computer art scene in 1967 with several key works. First was his piece with James Shaffer, Sine Curve Man, which was the Computers and Automation first prize winner for 1967.

name: “Hummingbird” by Charles Csuri
desc: One of the earliest computer animations, Csuri moved away from the geometric abstraction of his European computer art peers, introducing figuration to computer art.

name: “Untitled (Micro Innovation)” by Georg Nees
desc: This work, from Nees’s series exploring the polygon from 1965-1968, investigates the relationship between “order and complexity” and "aesthetic measure.” These concepts were developed by Abraham Moles and Max Bense in Europe, drawing on George David Birkhoff’s aesthetic measure and on Claude Shannon’s information theory at Bell Labs.

name: “Verifying star” by Donald K. Robbins
desc: This piece by the pioneer computer artist Robbins celebrates the intricacy of geometric forms and their ability to capture nature’s inner beauty.

name: “Matrix Multiplication Series 31” by Frieder Nake
desc: This colored plotter drawing features four squares with algorithmically assigned colors. An edition of this series is included in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

name: “Computer Nude (Studies in Perception I)” by Leon Harmon and Ken Knowlton
desc: Created by Harmon and Knowlton at Bell Labs, this computer generated photomural of a reclining nude, twelve feet long, was made entirely of abstract symbols.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: “Running Cola is Africa” by Computer Technique Group (CTG)
desc: This iconic plotter drawing, exhibited at Cybernetic Serendipity, was created in 1967 and 1968 by CTG at the IBM Scientific Data Centre in Tokyo.

name: “The Science of Art” by Robert E. Mueller
desc: The book voices the growing sense amongst some artists that science was encroaching upon the art world.

name: “Research Center Art Technology and Society” Founded in Amsterdam by Robert Hartzema, Tjebbe van Tijen
desc: This early digital art group that would last until 1969 published research reports on issues such as enhanced collaboration between artists and scientists.
subjects: research center art technology and society

name: Gyorgy Kepes Establishes the “Center for Advanced Visual Studies” (CAVS) at MIT
desc: The Center was established at The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) by Kepes “to bring artists from around the world to collaborate with MIT’s community of scientists and engineers, [in order] to produce works using new directions in technological approach.” It was attempted to create a community of innovators, providing opportunities for artists such as Nam June Paik and Stan Vanderbeek.

name: “Generative Photography” at Bielefeld Kunsthaus
desc: Gottfried Jäger, Hein Gravenhorst, Kilian Breier and Pierre Cordier introduced the art world to the concept of generative photography with this eponymous exhibit at Bielefeld Kunsthaus.

name: “Computer Graphic” Exhibition at Brno House of Arts
desc: Curated by Jiří Valoch, this was the first exhibition of computer art in Easter Europe. The exhibition featured works from pioneers A.

name: Aristid Lindenmayer Introduces the World to “L-Systems”
desc: The Hungarian theoretical biologist and botanist, Lindenmayer, developed Lindenmayer systems (or L-systems) to mathematically describe the growth processes of plant development.

name: Douglas Engelbart Gives “The Mother of all Demos”
desc: This monumental demonstration showed how computers could “amplify human capabilities,” paving the way for modern user interface and experience, changing the way computers were used to make art forever.
subjects: institute of electrical and electronics engineers (ieee)

name: "On the Path to Computer Art” by the Parallel Group
desc: The parallel group held the exhibition On the Path to Computer Art in conjunction with a joint conference of MIT and the Technical University, Berlin in the summer of 1968.
subjects: on the path to computer art

name: Leslie Mezei Develops SPARTA
desc: In an attempt to make graphic design on computers more accessible to those without programming experience, Mezei developed the early computer graphics language SPARTA in 1968.

name: First Publication of “Leonardo”
desc: Founded by kinetic artist and astronautical pioneer Frank Malina in Paris, the importance and relevance of Leonardo to this day cannot be overstated.

name: Centro de Estudios de Artes y Comunicación (CEAC), later CAyC, Established in Buenos Aires
desc: CAyC played an important role in the development of Systems art and Conceptual art in Latin America. It was led by Jorge Glusberg from its 1968 founding, as CEAC, until his death in 2012.

name: Foundation of the Computer Arts Society
desc: Founded by Alan Sutcliffe, George Mallen and John Lansdown, the Society (1968-1985) was formed “to encourage the creative use of computers and to allow the exchange of information in this area.” For decades CAS has aimed to advance the understanding of digital and electronic media’s role in the arts.

name: “Computer Art: Media Transformation through Electronics” by CTG
desc: This show by Computer Technique Group (CTG) was held at the Tokyo Gallery, Ginza Miyuki Avenue.
subjects: computer art: media transformation through electronics

name: Notable computer artworks
desc: Return to Square A, Computer Technique Group Return to Square B, Computer Technique Group Shot Kennedy No. 1, Computer Technique Group Christmas Wreath—Computer Style, Maughan S.

name: “Plexus” and “The Snail” by Kerry Strand and Larry Jenkins
desc: The Snail by Kerry Strand, and Symplexity by Kerry Strand and Larry Jenkins, were important early computer-generated drawings for their curvilinear forms.

name: “Quad III” by Robert Mallary
desc: This computer-generated sculpture was first exhibited at the Whitney Museum and is now in the Tate collection; it was Quad I that was shown at Cybernetic Serendipity in London.

name: Vera Molnár Begins her Computer Art Phase with the “Interruptions” Series
desc: Molnár’s earliest computer art phase began in 1968 with a short series of untitled plotter drawings and the open series Interruptions (1968–69).
