name: Lillian Schwartz Begins Her Computer Art Career
desc: According to the biography on her website, “Schwartz began her computer art career as an offshoot of her merger of art and technology, which culminated in the selection of her kinetic sculpture, Proxima Centauri, by The Museum of Modern Art for its epoch-making 1968 Machine Exhibition.” She would soon after become an artist in residence at Bell Labs, working with Leon Harmon and Kenneth Knowlton.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Georg Nees Completes His PhD Thesis (In German), “Generative Computergraphik”
desc: The pioneer’s doctoral thesis was instrumental in our continued association with computers and generative art.

name: Lee Harrison III Builds Scanimate
desc: The Scanimate was an analog computer animation system that succeeded Harrison’s earlier ANIMAC.

name: “The Art of Computer Programming” by Donald E. Knuth
desc: The first volume of a foundational seven-volume series of books seeks to “train the reader in various skills that go into the programmer’s craft.” Knuth continues publishing additional volumes to this day, as the series is still incomplete; the most recent is Volume 4B (2023).

name: “Pénétrables” by Jesús Rafael Soto
desc: The Venezuelan kinetic art pioneer sought to involve the viewer physically with his immense and immersive Pénétrables installations.

name: “Sound Activated Mobile” by Edward Ihnatowicz
desc: Sound Activated Mobile (SAM) was a pioneering cybernetic sculpture that responded to its surrounding audio environment.

name: “TV as a Creative Medium”, at the Howard Wise Gallery
desc: This group exhibition, featuring artists such as Nam June Paik and Eric Siegel, saw TV as “the root of the cause of all these changes that [were] transforming our civilization.” This was an important exhibition in the development of video art, which was beginning to boom as video-recording technology was becoming cheaper and smaller, notably the Sony Portapak.

name: “Kleiner Sonnenuntergang (Small Sunset)” by Dieter Roth
desc: This important example in the history of chance in art and material generative art was created with perishable, common materials that were meant to decay over time, such as paper and foodstuffs.

name: “Beyond Modern Sculpture: The Effects of Science and Technology on the Sculpture of Our Time” by Jack Burnham
desc: The former Artforum editor played a key role in advancing the role of technology in art.

name: “Bit International” Magazine Begins Publication
desc: This New Tendencies magazine published by Zagreb City Galleries would release nine editions from 1968-1972. The Zagreb group would go on to organize the iconic Tendencies 4 in 1969. 1968 saw the release of “Bit No.

name: Some More Beginnings at the Brooklyn Museum, New York
desc: From November 26, 1968, to January 5, 1969, the Brooklyn Museum hosted Some More Beginnings, an exhibition presented by Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.).
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: “Kunst Und Computer” Exhibition at Vienna Sparkasse
desc: Vienna’s first computer art exhibition was curated by Otto Beckmann and featured the works of artists such as Herbert Franke, Frieder Nake, Georg Nees and Kurd Alsleben.

name: “Art and Cybernetics” Exhibition by CAyC
desc: The Centro de Arte y Comunicación (CAyC) hold their first international exhibition, in August and September 1969, showing work by Japanese, British, American and Argentine artists.

name: “Slant One” by Auro Lecci
“The Philosophy of Computer Art” by Haruki Tsuchiya
desc: Published in Computers and Automation, the brief article by Tsuchiya stresses the importance of process, randomness and system in computer art.

name: “Tendencies 4: Computers and Visual Research” at Museum of Contemporary Art Zagreb
desc: Tendencies 4: Computers and Visual Research was a groundbreaking exhibition held at the Gallery of Contemporary Art, Zagreb, today the Museum of Contemporary Art, showcasing the convergence of art and digital technology.

name: “Computerkunst - On the Eve of Tomorrow” Exhibition in Hanover
desc: Curated by Käthe Schröder at Galerie Kubus in Hannover, Germany, On the Eve of Tomorrow played an important role of popularizing computer art in Central Europe, as it was one of the largest such showcases in the region.
subjects: computerkunst — on the eve of tomorrow

name: Notable Computer Artworks
subjects: computer sculpture: six levels of cybernetics

name: “When Attitudes Become Form” at Kunsthalle, Bern
“Event One” by Computer Arts Society
desc: The first exhibition of the newly formed Computer Arts Society, Event One took place at the Royal College of Art. It impacted the development of the “creative use of computers in the arts,” particularly in the UK.

name: Xerox PARC Founded
desc: Xerox’s Palot Alto Research Center (PARC) was founded by Dr. George Pake.

name: ARPANET Goes Live, Precursor to the Internet
desc: The Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (ARPANET), precursor to the modern Internet, went live in September 1969, with four host computers connected by year’s end.

name: Computer Technique Group (CTG) Disbands
desc: At the end of 1969 the group decided to disband citing difficulties collaborating with each other.

name: Sol LeWitt Brings His Wall Drawings
desc: Begun in 1968 and continuing until his death in 2007, LeWitt’s seminal Wall Drawings were important examples of randomness in systems-based art.

name: “A Philosophy of Computer Art” by Dominic Lopes
desc: This book critically examines the unique characteristics of computer art, setting a new theoretical foundation for understanding its place in the art world.

name: International Psytech Art exhibition – “Electromagica ’69”
desc: The landmark exhibition and symposium held at the Sogetsu Hall in Tokyo featured Kinetic, Light, and Lumino-Kinetic works from Japan, Western Europe and North America.

name: CTG Participates in the Paris Biennale
desc: The Japanese Computer Technique Group (CTG) showed three plotted works along with an early computer animation, Computer Movie No. 1, “produced by filming their computer-generated images on an IBM 2250 CRT.”

name: “Reticulárea” by Gego (Gertrud Goldschmidt)
desc: Gego’s best-known work, Reticulárea was exhibited at the Museo de Bellas Artes, Caracas.

name: “Hello” by Allan Kaprow
desc: This interactive video happening utilized the Boston-area closed-circuit TV network with Kaprow as director.

name: “Cross Talk Intermedia” at the Yoyogi Gymnasium, Tokyo
desc: This exhibition was an attempt to promote a dialogue between American and Japanese artists experimenting with technology and “intermedia.” It featured several artists associated with Jikken Kobo movement.

name: “Square Tops” by Wen-Ying Tsai
desc: The Chinese born Wen-Ying Tsai was a pioneer of cybernetic and kinetic sculpture. His 1969 works, Harmonic Sculpture and Square Tops exemplify his critical contributions to the development of electronic art from kinetic sculpture.

name: The Systems Group Founded
desc: Inspired by Constructivism, Jeffrey Steele, a former Op Art painter, founded the Systems group, which included artists such as John Ernest, Gillian Wise and Malcolm Hughes.

name: “Sonakinatography I Movement #III for Multi-Media” by Channa Horwitz
desc: Sonakinatography is the breakthrough series by Horwitz, meaning “sound,” “motion” and “notation.” On graph paper, she plotted the motion of eight entities over time with colors and numbers in 8x8 square grids.

name: Thomas Wilfred, Lumia Suite, Opus 158
desc: Commissioned by the Museum of Modern Art, this piece went on view at the museum’s 1964 reopening and stayed on display until 1981 before being disassembled.

name: Thomas Wilfred Begins His Lumia Public Performances
desc: Lumia is an Lumino-kinetic art form invented by Wilfred and performed on a device called a clavilux or “color organ.” These compositions of light were infinitely changing and had the appearance of a colorful aurora borealis.

name: Euclid’s Elements
desc: Considered one of the most influential and long-used textbooks of all time, Elements remains a key work in geometry’s logical development.

name: Computer Art Meets the Venice Biennale
desc: In a sign that computer art was gaining greater acceptance and recognition, some of the movement’s leading artists participated in the first computer art exhibition at the Venice Biennale.

name: Gene Youngblood Publishes the Seminal Expanded Cinema
desc: Youngblood’s Expanded Cinema was an expansive survey of the use of computers and code to create film. The book was critical to the development of media and video art.

name: Information exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art
desc: This landmark Conceptual art exhibition reinforced the dematerialization of the art object. Kynaston McShine curated Information in consultation with art historian and critic Lucy Lippard.
subjects: six years: the dematerialization of the art object

name: 1970 Osaka World’s Fair Showcases Global Nature of Computer Art
desc: The Osaka Expo marked a pivotal turning point in post-war Japanese art history by marking an end to avant-garde movements and ushering in the era of new media art.

name: Howard Wise Gallery Closes
desc: The gallery, which had served as a, if not the, key supporter of technology and art-based practices, closed in 1971 after eleven years in operation.

name: Women Pioneers Bring Naturalism to Computer Art
desc: The decade of the ‘70s saw a group of Women pioneers, specifically Grace C. Hertlein, Joan Truckenbrod, Colette Bangert and Lillian Schwartz, infuse the computer art aesthetic with a more naturalist touch.

name: Georg Nees, Computergrafik Computerplastik (Computer Graphics Computer Sculpture) Portfolio
desc: This portfolio of lithographs based on Nees’s plotted and sculptural work from the ‘60s were based on the Information Aesthetics of Max Bense, whom Nees studied under at the University of Stuttgart.

name: Martin Gardner Publishes John Conway’s Game of Life in Scientific American
desc: Originally played by hand with counters and published by Martin Gardner, Conway’s Life is the best-known two-dimensional cellular automaton. It served as a foundational concept and source of inspiration for many generative artists.

name: Sonia Landy Sheridan Founds Generative Systems at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago
desc: Sheridan founded the Generative Systems program at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago that would continue for a decade.
subjects: school of the art institute of chicago

name: Early Computer Graphics Conferences Appear
desc: The spring of 1970 saw two of the first conferences dedicated to computer graphics. The first, Werkgroep voor Computers en Woord, Beeld en Geluid, took place in March in Delft and Amsterdam.
subjects: werkgroep voor computers en woord, beeld en geluid

name: Generación Automática de Formas Plásticas Exhibition at the Centro de Cálculo of the University of Madrid
desc: This computer art exhibition, curated by Ernesto García Camarero featured the contributions of early pioneers of the movement including E. Robert Ashworth, Auro Lecci, Leslie Mezei, Petar Milojević, Frieder Nake, Georg Nees, A.

name: Lewis Mumford’s The Pentagon Of Power: The Myth Of The Machine and Alvin Toffler’s Future Shock Take Pessimistic View on Technology
desc: These two books had a significant impact on views towards technology in the 1970s, challenging prevailing notions that technological progress was inherently positive and beneficial.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: “Art et ordinateur” by Abraham Moles and Marie-Luce André
desc: Abraham Moles and Marie-Luce André publish the book “Art et ordinateur,” an important work in the field of computational aesthetics that synthesizes the work of Claude Shannon’s theories into the work of cybernetics.

name: Frieder Nake’s Publicly Announces End to Computer Art Practice
desc: With his article, “There Should Be No Computer Art,” Nake announced the end of his work with the medium of computers.
subjects: there should be no computer art

name: The Senster by Edward Ihnatowicz
desc: This cybernetic sculpture was an important example of the intersection of kinetic art and cybernetic systems.

name: Journal Radical Software Begins Publication
desc: From 1970-1974 Radical Software, founded by Beryl Korot and Phyllis Gershuny with Ira Schneider as co-originator, was instrumental in the development and detailing of emerging trends in video, computer and media art.

name: City Painting by Grace C. Hertlein
desc: This work of about 1970 to 1972 by the woman computer art pioneer would go on to inspire contemporary artist Yazid, specifically his work Hashed Cities on fxhash.

name: Herbert W. Franke Publishes Computer Graphics—Computer Art
desc: The tide was turning against computers and technology in art by 1971. Howard Wise had permanently closed.

name: Jasia Reichardt’s Publishes The Computer in Art
desc: Reichardt’s follow up text to her landmark Cybernetic Serendipity show and catalog demonstrated her belief that computer art was a continuation of modernism’s transition to abstraction.

name: Arteônica Exhibition by Waldemar Cordeiro
desc: This Sao Paulo exhibition by the Brazilian pioneer, Cordeiro, helped ignite computer art in the region with Brazil and Argentina serving as the cultural bases.

name: Arte y Cibernética Held at Galería Bonino, Buenos Aires
desc: Held at Galería Bonino and organised by Jorge Glusberg, whose CAYC would prove instrumental in developing the computer art movement in South America during the 1970s.

name: Franke: “The Program Is the Art”
desc: Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art explains the importance of programming in computer art. Taylor describes how Herbert W.

name: Art and Technology Exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
desc: Five years in the making and organized by Maurice Tuchman, Art and Technology was an attempt to involve industrial firms (and their machinery) in the production of art.

name: James Seawright, Network III, 1971
desc: Between 1965 and 1971, the lumino-kinetic cybernetic sculptor Seawright created light and sound mechanical installations that were both emblematic of the techo-spirit of the time as well as deeply forward looking, anticipating interactive digital installations of two to three decades later.

name: Manfred Mohr’s First Solo Museum Exhibition of Computer-Generated Art
desc: Mohr’s show, Computer Graphics—Une Esthétique Programmée, was held at the ARC, Musée d’Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, curated by Pierre Gaudibert.
subjects: arc (musée d'art moderne de la ville de paris)
musée d'art moderne de la ville de paris

name: Tsai Wen-Ying, Umbrella
desc: Tsai Wen-Ying was important artist in the transition from cybernetic and lumino-kinetic to electronic art. Tsai began creating cybernetic sculptures composed of vibrating rods like Umbrella in 1966.

name: Key Tech Developments for Digital Generative Art
desc: 1. Intel develops the first commercially produced microprocessor, the Intel 4004. The first of many Intel CPUs. 2. A. Michael Noll develops scanned-display computer graphics Listen to [Peter Bauman’s interview with A.

name: Kenneth Martin, Chance and Order V, 1971-2
desc: Martin stands as an important figure in the material (non-digital) generative art movement, according to Philip Galanter. Beginning in 1949, he incorporated rules and chance into his material practice.

name: Myron Krueger, Psychic Space
desc: Another lumino-kinetic interactive installation, Psychic Space consisted of a pressure-sensitive floor that activated a sound and visual program on the walls.

name: Dennis Ritchie Develops the C Language
desc: Devised by Ritchie at Bell Laps as a language for the budding Unix operating system, C was an upgrade over the B language and derived from the typeless BCPL.

name: Harold Cohen’s early work exhibited at LACMA
desc: Cohen’s exhibition, Three Behaviors for the Partitioning of Space, at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art presented his early, pre-AARON computer drawings.
subjects: three behaviors for the partitioning of space

name: Manfred Mohr Begins Exploring the Cube
desc: With Cubic Limit I (1972-1975), Mohr begins his hallowed work focusing on the cube. He created an alphabet of signs from the twelve lines of a cube.

name: The Great Exhibition of London Lights Early Spark of the Arts & Crafts Movement
desc: Industrialization and Technology meet Art According to Frank Popper, “one can only speak of the direct influence of technology on art since the Industrial Revolution, and more particularly when its effects entered everyday life at the end of the 19th century through the progressive design movements known as Art Nouveau and its precedent, the Arts and Crafts movement, in England.” The first world’s fair, The Great Exhibition of London, kicks off the Modern Era of our Timeline due to its association with industrialization and its impact on the Arts and Crafts movement.

name: Alan Turing Proposes the “Turing Test”
desc: Originally called the imitation game, the Turing test is meant to determine whether a computer or AI can think like a human being. The test consists of a human interviewing both a person and machine.

name: Kurd Alsleben and Cord Passow Make Analog Computer Drawings
desc: Artist Kurd Alsleben in collaboration with physicist Cord Passow used an analogue computer (EAI 231 R) in Hamburg to create parametric generative art.

name: Trained Artists Intervene with Computers
desc: As the accessibility of computers improves, more trained artists begin directly intervening with the machines and code, such as Joan Truckenbrod and Colette Bangert.
subjects: school of the art institute of chicago
three behaviors for the partitioning of space

name: NTT InterCommunication Center Opens in Tokyo
desc: This cultural facility in Tokyo, dedicated to exploring the intersections of art, science, and technology, has been instrumental in creating a platform for generative art in Japan.

name: Inaugural Exhibition at bitforms: Casey Reas’s first commercial gallery showing
desc: This show is the first for the newly opened gallery, bitforms, which would help to reintroduce the fine art world to technology and art at the turn of the millennium.

name: hello world by Kazumasa Teshigawara (qubibi)
desc: Shown at the Museum of Digital Arts (MuDA) in Zurich several years later in 2017 and generating animated imagery in real-time, hello world explores the visual language of primordial beginnings.

name: Art Blocks Brings Generative Art On Chain
desc: Art Blocks Brings Generative Art On Chain If NFTs unlocked demand, then Art Blocks, founded by Erick “Snowfro” Calderon, provided a space for demand to meet supply, creating a community where artists could manifest the technological, artistic and conceptual advancements of human history to push boundaries in art.

name: Grenzgebiete der bildenden Kunst (“Frontiers of Fine Arts”) Exhibit at the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart
desc: This exhibition, according to Herbert W. Franke, was an example of “only a few events of purely artistically oriented institutions” displaying computer art at the time.

name: P-120-A Meta Language II by Manfred Mohr
desc: This work was heavily inspired by Max Bense’s generative aesthetics and, by extension, Noam Chomsky’s Syntactic Structures and his work with generative linguistics.

name: Important Early Publications Including Computer Art
desc: The following were three publications important to the development of computer art according to Herbert W. Franke: 1. La scienza e l’arte (ed.

name: Edward Lorenz Presents Paper on the Butterfly Effect
desc: A key text in the development of chaos theory and thus twentieth-century science, Lorenz “was the first to recognize what is now called chaotic behavior in the mathematical modeling of weather systems.” Chaos theory would play a critical role in the development of generative art according to academic Phil Galanter.

name: Robert E. Mueller Pans Computer Art
desc: Writing in Art in America and one of the few times computer art is mentioned by a major mainstream art publication, Mueller describes visual outputs from computers as “exceedingly poor and uninspiring.” This sentiment reflects the growing skepticism of the times regarding technology and art.

name: Surface Substitution on 36 Plates by Jennifer Bartlett
desc: This important work in both math and chance in art demonstrates how algorithmic approaches to material art could produce visually interesting patterns based on numbers.

name: Shigeko Kubota’s Video Diaries
desc: The Fluxus artist’s work with video diaries began in 1972. Kubota’s experimental approach combined performance, technology, and personal narratives, creating visually striking and thought-provoking works.

name: Atari Releases Pong
desc: A pioneer of electronic gaming, Nolan Bushnell commissioned Pong from the engineer Al Alcorn. Pong, one of the first successful video games of all time, introduced the world to interactive electronic entertainment.

name: M 3x3 by Analívia Cordeiro
desc: The seminal work of Brazilian video and computer art pioneer, Analivia Cordeiro, M 3x3 is not only a work of generative choreography, it is also a work of video art.

name: Arte y Computadoras by CAYC
desc: Held in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in cooperation with the University of Minnesota Minneapolis, Arte y Computadoras (“Art and computers in Latin America”) was part of CAYC’s exhibition at the International Conference on Computers in the Humanities (ICCH).
subjects: international conference on computers in the humanities (icch)

name: Malcolm Hughes Establishes Experimental Department at the Slade
desc: Hugely important and later renamed the Experimental and Computing Department and lasting until 1981, the department introduced computer and video fine art to the Slade School of Fine Art at University College London, influenced by Slade staff member titans and students such as Harold Cohen, Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi.

name: 1024 Colours by Gerhard Richter
desc: Inspired by hardware store paint color charts, this painting’s composition was determined by a randomly generated algorithm. This piece is part of a series started by Richter in the 1960s.

name: Xerox PARC Develops Alto Personal Computer
desc: On the cutting edge, the Alto had a bitmapped screen and pioneered the graphics-based display, mouse, windows and icons that later systems inherited.

name: Cybernetic ARTRIP in Tokyo
desc: Held at the Sony Building in Tokyo, this notable Japanese computer art exhibit famously featured Shiro Takahashi’s inflatable faces and hands that were computer controlled.

name: France Hosts International Computer Art Events
desc: The first such event, Art et Ordinateur, held in Bordeaux was a seminar and exhibition that showcased the work of artists such as Manfred Mohr.

name: Inaugural SIGGRAPH Conference Held
desc: Occurring during the National Sciences Foundation Workshop on Computer Graphics in Boulder, Colorado, the inaugural SIGGRAPH (Special Interest Group on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques) conference, held in July 1974, marked a pivotal moment in the intersection of art and technology.

name: The Computer Arts Society Organizes INTERACT: MACHINE: MAN: SOCIETY
desc: INTERACT: MACHINE: MAN: SOCIETY was an “eventibition” that took place over five days at Edinburgh University.

name: Vera Molnár First Solo Exhibition Transformations
desc: Held at the gallery of the Polytechnic of Central London, Molnár’s Transformations is a series of 21 drawings plotted in black ink on white paper on a Benson plotter.

name: Vera Molnár Develops “Molnart” Software
desc: Molnár developed “Molnart” with her husband François Molnár between the years 1974 and 1976. The software program enabled engagement in expérimentation picturale systématique (“systematic pictorial experimentation”).

name: Ruth Leavitt Publishes Groundbreaking Book, Artist and Computer
desc: Leavitt’s book explores the relationship between artist and computer in depth. She sent a list of questions to dozens of contemporary computer artists. The responses she then compiled into a book.

name: PostScript Language Developed
desc: PostScript, which would go on to influence the Processing language created by Casey Reas and Ben Fry 25 years later, was developed by Dr John Warnock at PARC, Xerox’s research arm.

name: Alvy Ray Smith Develops PAINT
desc: From Smith’s 1978 Technical Memo No. 7 at the New York Institute of Technology’s Computer Graphics Lab: “Paint is a menu-driven computer program for handpainting two-dimensional images in full color.

name: Hypertransformations by Vera Molnár
desc: One of Molnár’s most recognizable phases (1975-76), Hypertransformations “examines the effects of minor changes in parameters of the x- and y-axis to regular squares.” The works are similar to (Dés)Ordres except features only series of concentric squares instead of many on a grid.

name: Untitled Computer Assisted Drawing by Paul Brown
desc: Displayed at the Victoria and Albert Museum’s 2018 exhibition, Chance and Control: Art in the Age of Computers, Brown’s work is composed of black linear forms or “tiles” on a white background, showing how simple forms can combine to create dense patterns.
subjects: chance and control: art in the age of computers

name: Altair 8800 Microcomputer
desc: First truly personal computers to sell in large numbers. It was available in 1975 for $397 as a kit and appeared on the January 1975 cover of Popular Electronics.

name: Brian Eno Releases “Discreet Music”
desc: Eno’s album Discreet Music employed techniques for randomness to compose generative music that resemble and build upon the work of artists such as John Cage, Terry Riley and Steve Reich.

name: The 2nd International Conference on Computers and the Humanities (ICCH/2) at the University of Southern California
desc: Organized by Grace C. Hertlein, ICCH/2 was the largest computer art exhibition held in the United States at that point. It showcased computer made film, graphics and music.
subjects: international conference on computers in the humanities (icch)

name: Mandelbrot Coins the Term Fractal
desc: Benoit Mandelbrot coined the term fractal while working at IBM. Using computer generated images to illustrate his mathematically derived concepts, he was consolidating hundred of years of mathematical theory.

name: Computer Graphics by Melvin L. Prueitt
desc: Prueitt’s book showcases the PICTURE computer program that he developed at the Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory.

name: Noisefields by Steina and Woody Vasulka
desc: This audiovisual work of “video noise” was created by the electronic art pioneers Steina and Woody Vasulka who co-founded The Kitchen in 1971 where they helped non-technical artists incorporate technology into their practice.

name: Videoplace by Myron Krueger
desc: Deemed “decades ahead of its time” by Casey Reas, Krueger developed Videoplace for nearly twenty years. This interactive computer system allowed users to engage with virtual environments through body movements and gestures.

name: Science and Technology in the Arts: A Tour through the Realm of Science/Art by Stewart Kranz
desc: This comprehensive exploration of the intersection between science, technology and the arts provides a captivating journey into various disciplines, including visual arts, music, theater, film and literature, to reveal the profound influence of scientific advancements on artistic expression.

name: Muriel Cooper Founds the Visible Language Workshop
desc: Derived from a course taught by Cooper at MIT, “Messages and Means,” the Visible Language Workshop (VLW) took a multi-disciplinary approach to design.

name: IBM Produces First Portable Computer
desc: The IBM SCAMP Microcomputer was a prototype of one of the first portable computers, the IBM 5100 which would be announced in 1975.

name: International Computer Arts Festival at The Kitchen, New York
desc: This festival featured panels, films, graphics and music made or inspired by computers.

name: Six Years: The Dematerialization of the Art Object from 1966 to 1972 by Lucy Lippard
desc: Lucy Lippard’s book Six Years: The Dematerialization of the Art Object from 1966 to 1972 was a seminal publication that had a significant influence on contemporary generative art.
subjects: six years: the dematerialization of the art object

name: Thomas DeFanti Founds Electronic Visualization Lab (EVL)
desc: Founded by Thomas DeFanti and Dan Sandin, the Electronic Visualization Lab (EVL) is still in existence today. EVL is a research lab at the University of Illinois at Chicago focused on computer science and advanced technologies.

name: Vera Molnár Begins her Iconic (Des)Ordres Series
desc: One of Molnár’s most recognizable series of works, (Des)Ordres consists of a grid of concentric squares with random distortions that highlight the distinction between order and chaos.

name: Art et Informatique by Maison de la Culture d’Angers
desc: The festival featured work by some of the leading computer graphics and photography artists of the time including: Vera Molnar, Hein Gravenhorst, Herbert W. Franke, Manfred Mohr, Gottfried Jager, Frieder Nake and Georg Nees.

name: The Bat-Sheva-Seminar on the Interaction of Art and Science
desc: Organized in Jerusalem by the computer artist Vladimir Bonačić, a member of Leonardo’s editorial advisory board, the seminar was attended by Jonathan Benthall, Herbert W. Franke, Frank Joseph Malina, Abraham A. Moles, A.
subjects: bat-sheva seminar on the interaction of art and science

name: Frieder Nake Publishes Ästhetik als Informationsverarbeitung (“Aesthetics as Information Processing”)
desc: According to Herbert W. Franke, this was “probably the most important book [on early computer art].” The book aimed to relate the Information Aesthetics of Max Bense and Abraham Moles to Computer graphics.

name: TV Buddha and TV Garden by Nam June Paik
desc: TV Buddha remains one of Paik’s signature works, a video sculpture consisting of a seated Buddha facing a television screen where it watches an image of itself.

name: Incomplete Open Cubes by Sol LeWitt
desc: In this seminal work, LeWitt demonstrates his mastery of seriality, exploring the 122 ways of making an incomplete cube.

name: Jasia Reichardt Captures Key Theme of ‘70s Computer art: The Artist-Programmer
desc: According to Jasia Reichardt and Grant Taylor, the 1970s marked the era of the artist-programmer. The practitioners of computer art began shifting away from the engineers and scientists who began the movement a decade earlier.

name: The Dinner Party by Judy Chicago
desc: A landmark work of feminist art made from 1974 to 1979, this installation consists of a large, triangular shaped banquet table set with symbolic place settings representing 39 historically significant women.

name: P-154-C by Manfred Mohr
desc: Work indicative of Mohr’s early to mid-70s work exploring and deconstructing the cube.

name: Graffiti Emerges as an Art Form
desc: Graffiti art has ancient roots but the modern form began in the '60s in the Northeastern United States. By the early '70s in New York, young people were writing their names and street numbers across the city.

name: Motorola Begins Developing First Handheld Mobile Phone
desc: Motorola annonuced the development of the Dyna-Tac. It would not commercially available, however, until 1983. The development of mobile devices is seen by artist Casey Reas as an important pre-condition for NFTs.

name: Remington Releases the Standard Number 2 Typewriter
desc: One of the world’s first commercially successful typewriters, the Remington and Sons Standard Number 2 typewriter featured a QWERTY keyboard, which it helped to establish as the standard to this day.

name: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak Develop the Apple I and Found Apple
desc: Apple Computer Company was founded on 1 April 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne, with the goals of making computers more user-friendly for a mass market.

name: Musicolour (1953–57), Gordon Pask
desc: Exhibited at Cybernetic Serendipity, this ahead of its time cybernetic sculpture anticipated interactivity in electronic art.

name: Grace Hertlein Begins Editing *Computer Graphics and Art*
desc: Hertlein’s Computer Graphics and Art played a crucial role in the development of generative art history.

name: Alan Kay and Adele Goldberg of PARC Publish "Personal Dynamic Media”
desc: This paper conceived of the laptop and tablet computers decades before their existence.

name: “3-D Computer Animation” by Charles Csuri
desc: This book chapter by one of the founders of computer art would have a significant impact on the development of 3D computer graphics in the coming decades.

name: Arbitrary Fragments by Barbara Latham
desc: This pioneering work of video art saw Latham commenting on the inherently fragmented nature of video. The work features extensively manipulated and processed visuals showcasing this fragmentation.

name: Arts et Informatique organized by the Swedish Cultural Centre in Paris
desc: Part two of three successive exhibitions by the Swedish Cultural Center that accompanied seminars in Paris between 1977 and 1979.

name: Harold Cohen Exhibits AARON at the Stedelijk Museum
desc: Now referred to as his “turtle,” AARON was showcased in a one-person show at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam across 1977 and 1978.

name: ICCH Held at the University of Waterloo in Canada
desc: This mostly academic conference was also held in conjunction with relevant computer graphics conferences of the time.
subjects: international conference on computers in the humanities (icch)

name: L’ordinateur et les arts visuels by François Molnar
desc: This book on computers and the visual arts published by Centre Pompidou and the University of Paris brings together academic texts from the field. One of the major texts is by Vera Molnár’s husband, François.

name: P-196-A and P-197-A by Manfred Mohr
desc: Mohr produced this series of computer-generated drawings from 1977, within the Cubic Limit II phase. The series consisted of images of deconstructed single cubes. Dissected, the cubes were not symmetrical.

name: Computergraphik by Lothar Limbeck
desc: This master’s thesis, Computergrafik, Ein Lehr- und Lernbuch (“Computer graphics, a text and learning book”), was a survey of computer graphics.

name: Apple Introduces Apple II
desc: One of the first mass-produced “microcomputers,” the Apple II helped begin the personal computer crazy in the late 1970s, revolutionizing computing and computer art forms.

name: I Ching Later Read as Binary
desc: First written between 1,000 to 750 BCE, I Ching, also known as the Book of Changes, is an ancient Chinese divination text.

name: Artificial Versifying by John Peter
desc: In [John Peter’s book](https://digitalarchive.tpl.ca/objects/332679/artificial-versifying-or-the-schoolboys-recreation--a-n) [Artificial Versifying](https://digitalarchive.tpl.ca/objects/332679/artificial-versifying-or-the-schoolboys-recreation--a-n), the English mathematician describes a simple procedure that could be used to make generative poetry in Latin.

name: Eureka Exhibited at London’s Egyptian Hall
desc: John Clark’s Latin verse generating machine, Eureka, was a full mechanized version of [John Peter’s book,](https://digitalarchive.tpl.ca/objects/332679/artificial-versifying-or-the-schoolboys-recreation--a-n) [Artificial Versifying](https://digitalarchive.tpl.ca/objects/332679/artificial-versifying-or-the-schoolboys-recreation--a-n), from 1677 and earlier in this Timeline.

name: Richard Williams Develops Art1
desc: Patrick Frank’s book, https://www.amazon.com/Sharing-Code-Frederick-Hammersley-Computer/dp/0890136556, draws attention to this fascinating early collaboration in computer art history.
subjects: sharing code: art1, frederick hammersley, and the computer

name: Cybernetic Symbiosis, Berkeley: Lawrence Hall of Science
desc: Organized by artist and California State University, Chico Computer Science professor, Grace C.

name: Art of the Space Era – Museum of Art, Huntsville, Alabama
desc: Held at the Huntsville Museum of Art in the United States, this two part exhibition curated by Thomas A.

name: Art and the Computer at the Worcester Art Museum and Computer Generated Art Exhibit at Old Dominion University
desc: These events held in the United States were “some of the most important computer graphics exhibitions of the last years,” according to Herbert W. Franke in Computer Graphics, Computer Art (1985).

name: Algorithmic Aesthetics: Computer Models for Criticism and Design in the Arts by George Stiny and James Gips
desc: Suggesting an algorithmic approach to aesthetics and criticism, George Stiny and James Gips continue the tradition of Max Bense and François Morellet.

name: Computer Art Grows
desc: According to Grant Taylor, In When the Machine Made Art, “By 1978, there were 30 times more computer art practitioners than a decade earlier.” One decade after its humble beginnings, computer art was growing.

name: Energized Artscience at the Chicago Museum of Science and Industry
desc: Curated by pioneer, Sonia Landy Sheridan who also wrote the show catalog, this exhibition at the Museum of Science and Industry does not have much existing information about it. Anymore would be greatly appreciated.

name: The Vasulka’s: Steina: Machine Vision; Woody: Description at the Albright-Knox Art Gallery
desc: Curated by Linda Cathcart, this exhibition featured the work of artists and partners, Steina and Woody Vasulka, pioneers of video art.

name: Douglas Hofstadter’s Publishes Book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
desc: This book exploring the latest trends in math, logic and computer language, would greatly influence artist Roman Verostko.

name: Jim Blinn Simulates Voyager Probe for NASA’s JPL
desc: Jim Blinn’s simulation of the Voyager Probe’s flyby of Jupiter for NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) would have a significant impact on the development of digital art history.

name: Computer Graphics World begins publication
desc: Still in print today, Computer Graphics World (CGW) was started by Joel Orr after originally existing as a Newsletter.

name: Thomas DeFanti, Jay Fenton and Nola Donato Develop Zgrass
desc: An extension of Defanti’s GRASS, ZGRASS was used for generating 3D imagery and developed to be used on smaller, personal computers and gaming devices.

name: “Space Invaders,” “Asteroids” and “Pac Man” Released
desc: Sparking the first video game craze, the release of Space Invaders was followed by Asteroids (1979) and Pac-Man (1980).

name: The First ARS ELECTRONICA Festival Takes Place in Linz, Austria
desc: “With electronics, a progressive element has entered our technical world, whose influence is not limited to industry and research, but intervenes in all areas of life.

name: Dance by Lucinda Childs
desc: By the legendary generative choreographer Lucinda Childs, this piece would be exhibited for the first time in 2009 at the Whitney Museum.

name: Frank J Malina Publishes Visual Art, Mathematics, and Computers
desc: This book contained Malina’s papers he published in the journal Leonardo. Herbert W. Franke called Malina a “patron of art technology” in 1985, four years after Malina’s death in 1981.

name: Informatrix by Edward Zajec
desc: This book by Zajec was published in 1979 from work he developed between 1970 and 1978. Informatrix was also a series of works by Zajec that he worked on over the course of nearly thirty years between 1970 and 1996.

name: C++ Developed by Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Laboratories
desc: One of the most popular programming languages of the 1990s and still widely used today, C++ began in 1979 with Bjarne Stroustrup’s arrival at the “1127 Computing Science Research Center of AT&T Bell Laboratories.” After five years, the first C++ language reference manual was internally published in 1984 and commercially released in 1985.

name: Konkrete Kunst: 50 Jahre Entwicklung, Helmhaus Zürich
desc: This iconic exhibition featured Concrete art of the last fifty years, an exhibition that by itself could nearly tell the story of this movement to this point in 1960.

name: Larry Cuba, Two Space
desc: Larry Cuba was a computer animation pioneer of the generation that directly followed John Whitney Sr. In 1975 Whitney invited Cuba to be the programmer on Arabesque. Earlier in the 1970s Cuba worked with Thomas DeFanti on GRASS.

name: Lorna, Lynn Hershman Leeson
desc: The artist describes Lorna, made from 1979 to 1984, as the first artwork to use laserdisc technology, and as an early interactive video art disc.

name: Traditionally Trained Artist, Mark Wilson, Buys Microcomputer to Make Art
desc: A representational beginning to the decade, which would be responsible for the explosion of “digital art” due to the emerging prevalence of computers and digital devices becoming smaller and entering homes.

name: Vera Molnár Develops Her “Machine Imaginaire”
desc: Meaning the “imaginary computer,” Molnár’s “machine imaginaire” is the now famous concept that she developed to imagine a computer to expand her creative process.

name: John Whitney Sr. Makes the Vertigo Titles with an Analog Computing Device
desc: After Hitchcock hired John Whitney to create the opening animation for his film, Vertigo, Whitney used a WWII-era “M5 gun director” targeting computer that required five people to operate.

name: https://el.media.mit.edu/logo-foundation/what_is_logo/history.html
desc: Designed by Wally Feurzeig, Seymour Papert and Cynthia Solomon, Logo was a general purpose programming language that was hugely important to the development of computer art.

name: Thomas Defanti Develops Animation Language GRASS (Graphics Symbiosis System)
desc: Completed as DeFanti’s doctoral work at Ohio State University, this landmark early computer animation language that was used by Larry Cuba to produce the graphics for the training sequence for the Rebel attack on the Death Star in Star Wars.

name: Bell Labs Team Discovers the Transistor
desc: Replacing the vacuum tube-concept of ENIAC, the discovery of the transistor by the team of Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain at Bell Labs sparked a revolution in electronics.

name: Jack St. Clair Kilby at Texas Instruments and, independently, Robert Noyce at Fairchild Arrive at the Integrated Circuit
desc: Kilby demonstrated his device in 1958, Noyce’s design following in 1959. The integrated circuit was a breakthrough in electronics that sparked the miniaturization of the industry.

name: MIT Demonstrates the Whirlwind Computer
desc: Begun in the mid-1940s under Jay Forrester at MIT to drive a programmable flight simulator for the Office of Naval Research, Whirlwind was demonstrated processing live radar data in September 1950.

name: Grace Murray Hopper Invents General Programming Languages
desc: Grace Hopper is one of the most important pioneers in the development of computer programming. Hopper pioneered the concept of automatic programming and in 1952 she developed the first compiler (A-0).

name: Around Is Around by Norman McLaren
desc: A pioneering work in the development of proto-computer abstract animation, Around Is Around, made with Evelyn Lambart and Chester Beachell, is a ten-minute long animated film that was groundbreaking for its time.

name: John McCarthy Introduces LISP
desc: John McCarthy at MIT introduced the programming language LISP (List Processing) in 1960. He published the language in his seminal paper in on recursive functions in programming.

name: computer grafik by Georg Nees and Frieder Nake at Galerie Wendelin Niedlich in Stuttgart (Germany)
desc: Opening November 5, 1965, computer grafik was Europe’s first computer art exhibition outside of a university and third ever public show. It was the third and final of the three famous 1965 shows.

name: Giorno Poetry Systems Founded
desc: John Giorno’s [Poetry Systems](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/john-giorno), “a nonprofit production company designed to introduce new, innovative poetry to wider audiences,” reflects Giorno’s belief that poetry, within the context of Pop-Art ideas, lagged behind other art forms in terms of media and inventiveness.

name: Joseph Weizenbaum publishes ELIZA
desc: The early natural language processing (NLP) computer program ELIZA is published by Joseph Weizenbaum, a computer scientist and MIT professor.

name: Poemfields by Stan VanDerBeek
desc: Having studied with the poet M.C.

name: The House of Dust by Alison Knowles
desc: Having collaborated with the likes of John Cage and Marcel Duchamp, Fluxus poet Alison Knowles teams up with composer James Tenney to write [The House of Dust](https://www.artforum.com/print/reviews/201207/alison-knowles-31967) – one of the earliest computer-generated poems, dated 1966 to 1968 by ZKM.

name: First Known Author Is a Woman
desc: The first author known by name was a woman: Enheduanna (fl. ca. 2300 BCE), daughter of Akkadian king Sargon and high priestess at the temple of the moon god in Ur, southern Mesopotamia.

name: Oracle at Delphi
desc: Scholars and travelers flock to Delphi, the most important shrine in Ancient Greece, to ask questions about the future and await, in exchange for gold and gifts, enigmatic replies from the Pythia, priestess of Apollo.

name: Library of Alexandria Established
desc: Library of Alexandria is established around the mission of “holding in one place all of the knowledge ever accumulated by man,” the world’s “memory bank”; the Ptolemic dynasty grows the library by decreeing that any book brought into the city be immediately copied by scribes, and taking measures to preclude rivals from collecting books.

name: Johannes Gutenberg’s Printing Press
desc: Johannes Gutenberg begins developing the mechanised moveable type printing press that would kick off Europe’s Printing Revolution, capable of producing up to 3600 pages per day and significantly reducing the cost of publishing and distributing literature.

name: “Tradition and the Individual Talent” by T.S. Eliot
desc: T.S.

name: Jack Kerouac Introduces Phrase “Beat Generation”
desc: Writing in response to the atrocities of WWII, the Beat Poets (including Allen Ginsberg and Lawrence Ferlinghetti) rebel against convention and seek to expand consciousness via experiments in automated writing, including hallucinogenics, spiritual rituals, and aleatory techniques meant to empower spontaneity and unfetter truth from the constraints of human reason.

name: Philo Farnsworth Invents the “Image Dissector”
desc: One of the most celebrated and prolific inventors of all time, Farnsworth was the quintessential “mad scientist” and inspiration for Professor Farnsworth on TV series Futruama.

name: Divisibility I by Manfred Mohr
desc: Divisibility I is a series that Mohr began in 1980 and would last until 1984. Again, Mohr returns to the cube as his main point of departure and inspiration.

name: Harold Cohen’s Arnolfini Series
desc: This [series of plotter drawings created by Cohen’s AARON](https://dam.org/museum/artists_ui/artists/cohen-harold/arnolfini/) were exhibited at the Arnolfini Gallery in Bristol, England.

name: “Portrait of the Artist As a Young Computer” by Grace Glueck
desc: As Grant Taylor points out, the title of this essay by art critic Grace Glueck in the New York Times is both a nod to James Joyce “as well as a parallel to the first article that pushed computerized art into the realm of popular culture: John R.
subjects: portrait of the artist as a young computer
portrait of the machine as a young artist

name: The Computer/The Artist exhibitions at the Long Beach Museum of Art
desc: [This exhibition in Long Beach, California](https://www.vasulka.org/archive/ExhFest12/LongBeachMOA/artist&comp.pdf), sought to present “computer-generated video, installation and static artworks.

name: SIGGRAPH’s Exhibition of Computer Art
desc: The third iteration of a computer art exhibition at the annual [SIGGRAPH conference’s Exhibition of Computer Art](https://digitalartarchive.siggraph.org/wp-content/uploads/1983/01/SIGGRAPH1983_Art_Show_Catalog.pdf.pdf) was its most successful yet, [traveling to](https://mediaburn.org/arts-culture/image-processing/early-siggraph-art-shows-1981-1985/) “over 30 locations throughout the U.S., Canada, France, Italy, and Japan” well into 1984.

name: Growth by Yoichiro Kawaguchi
desc: After working on his GROWTH algorithm for several years at this point, Kawaguchi exhibits his first artistic expression from the algorithm with Growth.

name: Cryptographer David Chaum First Proposes Blockchain-Like Protocol
desc: David Lee Chaum, an American pioneering cryptographer, released his dissertation, “Computer Systems Established, Maintained, and Trusted by Mutually Suspicious Groups.” This paper is considered the first known proposal for a blockchain protocol.

name: The Computer Image by Donald Greenberg, Aaron Marcus, Allan H. Schmidt, and Vernon Gorter
desc: The Computer Image was an important book in the burgeoning field of computer graphics, exploring its diverse applications.

name: Nam June Paik at Whitney Museum of American Art
desc: This Nam June Paik retrospective exhibition at the Whitney Museum celebrated the contributions of the pioneering video artist while also showcasing his latest work, V-yrimads.

name: L’Art et l’ordinateur in Paris
desc: Organized in Paris by CISI (Compagnie Inter-nationale de Service en Informatique), this event was a seminar and notable computer art exhibition for this period.
subjects: cisi (compagnie internationale de service en informatique)

name: Artists/Computers/Art at the Canada House Gallery, London
desc: This exhibition toured around four locations in 1982: London, Paris, Milton Keynes, England and Belfast, Northern Ireland. Please share if you have more information.

name: Montana by Jane Veeder
desc: This two-dimensional video by pioneering video artist Jane Veeder was developed with ZGRASS with a custom-made language she derived from arcade and video games.

name: Pantomation System by Tom De Witt
desc: An apprentice under Stan Vanderbeek, DeWitt Identified as a Dataist. He used algorithmic procedures and digital databases for his art, pioneering proto-net art.

name: The First Touchpad Introduced
desc: The Apollo Domain computer featured what’s believed to be the first touchpad. It was placed to the right of the keyboard.

name: Computer Rendering of Stochastic Models by Alain Fournier, Don Fussell, Loren Carpenter
desc: This famous paper in the history of computer graphics outlines the breakthrough that was fractal rendering, which is still hugely important to this day.

name: V-yramid by Nam June Paik
desc: Consisting of forty televisions, V-yramid was one of Paik’s largest video installations. It was made on behalf of the artist’s retrospective at the Whitney. Like much of Paik’s work, the piece focuses on duality: contemporary vs.

name: Roman Verostko Debuts The Magic Hand of Chance Series
desc: [The Magic Hand of Chance](http://www.verostko.com/downloads/compare/compare.html) [Series](http://www.verostko.com/downloads/compare/compare.html) (1982–85) was the legendary “Algorist’s” first foray into software work.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Pitfall! by David Crane
desc: A huge hit, Pitfall! was one of the Atari 2600’s signature games and one of 1982’s most popular. It was also a work of generative art, as it used an algorithmically generated world.

name: The Commodore 64 Released
desc: The Commodore 64, also known as the C64, was an 8-bit device that helped popularize the personal computer. It democratized home computing, bringing affordable and accessible technology to artists as well as hackers.

name: Art and Technology: Chicago Video at MoMA
desc: This exhibition at MoMA highlighted pioneering collaborations between artists and technology in the 1970s. By showcasing innovative computer-generated video works, it helped establish video art.

name: Bill Viola, Hatsu-Yume (First Dream)
desc: [This work by Viola](https://www.eai.org/titles/hatsu-yume-first-dream), a pioneer of video art, now stands in the collection of MoMA.

name: MTV Goes Live
desc: Music Television (MTV), the first 24-hour television station based on music videos, was launched on 1 August 1981, a seminal day in the history of digital creativity and storytelling.

name: High Technology Art: A Congressional Exhibition, Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.
desc: [This show](https://digitalartarchive.siggraph.org/exhibition/siggraph-1981-computer-culture-art-show-81/) was ​​exhibited at the Library of Congress in Washington D.C.
