desc: On March 1, Hicetnunc (HEN) officially launched its mainnet along with the OBJKT Swap Protocol on Tezos, which enabled NFT transactions.

name: The Third Mind by Beat Writer William Burroughs
desc: The Third Mind is published by Beat writer William Burroughs and the artist/poet/inventor Brion Gysin.

name: The VHS Recorder Brings Digital Media to the Home
desc: This seemingly benign event marks the beginning of what I argue is one of the most significant shifts in the history of human thinking: our love affair with digital devices.

name: Atari Founded
desc: Crticial to the turn in human thinking that made a generation of artists love computers. The Atari would encourage millions to fall in love with digital devices, particularly with its 1977 release of the Atari 2600.

name: Atari 2600 Released
desc: The Atari 2600 helped humanity transition from fearing computers a decade prior to loving them. It was also critical to the advancement of digital devices in our homes and the early Demoscene.

name: LaserDisc Introduced
desc: The first commercially successful optical storage device, the LaserDisc played an important in bringing digital media and changing the public’s mind about computers.

name: The Policeman’s Beard is Half-Constructed Published
desc: Billed as “the first book ever written by a computer,” [this experimental text](https://www.ubu.com/media/text/racter/racter_policemansbeard.pdf) comprised of computer prose and poetry is rooted in a program that writes without prompting, developed by William Chamberlain with Thomas Etter; illustrations by Joan Hall.

name: Media Archaeology: Approaches, Applications, and Implications by Erkki Huhtamo and Jussi Parikka
desc: Erkki Huhtamo’s concept of “Topos” is a fascinating idea in the realm of media studies.
subjects: media archaeology: approaches, applications, and implications

name: Dan Sandin Creates the Sandin Image Processor
desc: Arriving at the University of Illinois at Chicago, Sandin quickly leaves his mark by developing the revolutionary Sandin IP (Image Processor).

name: Duality and Co-Existence Exhibition, London
desc: Computer art pioneer Ernest Edmonds shows a generative work publicly for the first time.

name: Rise of ArtFutura
desc: As we begin the 1990s, a major trend, besides the rise of the Internet and the transition from “computer” to “digital” art, was a fascination with virtual reality.

name: First Assembly Party in Finland
desc: The winning PC demo of the inaugural Assembly Party, Unreal, marked a significant milestone in the demoscene community.

name: Scream Tracker 2 released by Future Crew
desc: The final major trend we begin this chapter with is the rise of the demoscene.

name: Breeding Forms on the Infinite Plane by William Latham
desc: Breeding Forms on the Infinite Plane, an exemplary work of Latham’s evolutionary art, creates biomorphic prints that resemble insect and crustacean forms.
subjects: breeding forms on the infinite plane

name: Mutations by William Latham
desc: William Latham’s [Mutations](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7sadS5wuOjU&ab_channel=HursleyMuseum) (1991-92) depicts a surreal journey of real-time evolutionary art, showcasing intricate breeding and growth processes through animated forms engaged in complex interactions.

name: MPEG 1 standard introduced
desc: The Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG) approved the MPEG-1 standard in November 1992, published as ISO/IEC 11172 in 1993, marking a pivotal moment in the history of digital audio and video compression that various groups had been working on for several years.

name: JPEG Standard Created
desc: Similar to the MPEG standard released the same year, the JPEG 1 standard (ISO/IEC 10918) was developed in 1992 as part of an effort to reduce the standard image file size, a process that began in 1986.

name: The Evolution of Form by William Latham
desc: Mentioned in Frank Popper’s Art of the Electronic Age, Latham’s work showcased his Mutator algorithm, combining chance mutations with creative choices to produce ever-evolving 3D forms of enormous complexity.

name: Fleshy Growth, Yoichiro Kawaguchi
desc: A monumentally important figure, Kawaguchi is a pioneer of computer 3D graphics and of procedural artificial-life work.

name: World Wide Web Tooling Complete
desc: “The 1990s witnessed a technological development of unprecedented speed for the digital medium—the so-called ‘digital revolution.’” -Christiane Paul in Digital Art (2003) The eminent Paul attributes this revolution to two factors: 1.

name: February: initial public release of Adobe Photoshop
desc: In Feb 1990, Adobe Photoshop, the ground-breaking image editing program, was made public. It changed the digital art world by providing strong tools for graphic design and photo manipulation.

name: Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta Describe a Cryptographically Secured Chain of Blocks
desc: A key moment in the development of blockchain technology and, thus, NFTs, Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta described a cryptographically secure chain of blocks, presented at CRYPTO ’90 and published in 1991.

name: Electric Sheep by Scott Draves
desc: Described [as](https://draves.org/aoae07/) a “collective intelligence,” this early example of machine learning in art was inspired by the evolutionary art work of Karl Sims.

name: Primordial Dance by Karl Sims
desc: Karl Sims unveiled this important work in the development of artificial life-based art, Primordial Dance, an experimental one-minute and 35-second code-based animation exploring abstract textures and colors.

name: Cruz-Neira, Sandin and DeFanti Begin Developing “CAVE”
desc: Carolina Cruz-Neira, Daniel J. Sandin and Thomas A. DeFanti, with Robert V. Kenyon and John C.

name: Fleischmann, Monika/Strauss, Wolfgang: Home of the Brain, virtual reality installation, 1989-1990
desc: Made between 1989 and 1990, the work by Monika Fleischmann and Wolfgang Strauss is described by the artists as the first artistic virtual reality installation.

name: The Virtual Museum by Jeffrey Shaw
desc: The Virtual Museum by Jeffrey Shaw emerged in Frankfurt, Germany, as a pioneering exploration of virtual reality.

name: Angels by Nicole Stenger
desc: Between 1989 and 1992, Stenger worked on Angels, the first immersive movie and an important early VR work. She developed the project at MIT and the University of Washington with an Advanced Visualizer.

name: Cercle Syncopé, Gillian Wise
desc: A member of Jeffrey Steele’s Systems Group (1969) and a former member of the British Constructivists, Wise was a prominent example of a systems artist, like Vera Molnar, moving from systematic thinking to programmed art with computers.

name: Sociotecture, Joan Truckenbrod
desc: One of four similar works in a series, this piece was included by Frank Popper in Art of the Electronic Age. Joan Truckenbrod’s Sociotecture series, initiated in 1991, explored the unseen dimensions of the human experience.

name: World Wide Web goes public
desc: January 1991 the first Web servers outside CERN itself were switched on. On August 6, 1991, Berners-Lee posted a short summary of the World Wide Web project on the alt.hypertext newsgroup.

name: Trojan Room Coffee Pot Camera Set Up at Cambridge
desc: The humble coffee pot sparked a technological revolution when computer scientists at the University of Cambridge invented the world’s first webcam.

name: Symposium: Art & Algorithm - Mind & Machine, 1991 (organized by Verostko)
desc: Roman Verostko, noted for his pioneering work such as The Magic Hand of Chance (1982), organized the Art & Algorithm Symposium at the Minneapolis College of Art and Design in 1991 (February 23-24).
subjects: images of the unseen from the worlds of art & science
minneapolis college of art and design

name: Keith Tyson begins working on ArtMachine
desc: Keith Tyson revolutionized the art world with ArtMachine in 1991, which he would work on for the next ten years.

name: Les Artistes et la lumiere, exhibition held in Rheims
desc: Included by Frank Popper in Art of the Electronic Age as an important exhibition in the development of electronic art [Popper 14], this exposition focused on works inspired by neon lighting.

name: Java Language Project Initiated at Sun Microsystems
desc: In the early ‘90s, Sun Microsystems began the development of the Java programming language, a watershed moment in the history of creative coding as it would be the basis for the upcoming Processing in ten years.

name: Publications
desc: Like the light going off after the chronicling of the Greek historian Herodotus around the 5th c. BCE, when the ancient world lost much of its color.
subjects: a selected chronology of computer art: exhibitions, publications, and technology
computer art—an oxymoron? views from the mainstream
critical questions for computer artists of the 1990s
in our own image: the coming revolution in photography

name: Computers and the Creative Process at the University of Oregon Museum of Art
desc: This exhibition actually traveled around North America to ten locations, from Oregon to Michigan and Texas to Canada. It would travel for two years until January 5, 1992. 31 artists were involved, including Professor Donna Cox.
subjects: university of oregon museum of art

name: Panspermia by Karl Sims
desc: This standout generative film by the icon Sims depicted an artificial world and remains an example of an early animation born from artificial evolution.

name: Emerging Forms 3 by Hillary Kapan
desc: Mentioned in Frank Popper’s Art of the Electronic Age and shown at the Artifices exhibition, and dated 1989 by the SIGGRAPH archive, this interactive animated work was produced from “a program generating changing forms from a scattered field of pixels,” according to Popper [89].

name: SOD by JODI
desc: The renowned net art duo JODI’s release of SOD represented a blend of their net.art roots, video game art and the video game cracking culture that led to the demoscene.

name: Legend I, Yoshiyuki Abe
desc: Legend I is the first piece in Yoshiyuki Abe’s renowned series, which ran until 2001 and was featured at ISEA94.

name: On Justifying the Hypothetical Nature of Art and the Non-Identicality within the Object World by Peter Weibel
desc: On Justifying the Hypothetical Nature of Art and the Non-Identicality within the Object World at Gallery Tanja Grunert, Cologne, presented an interactive computer installation that immersed visitors into a dark triangular space illuminated only by a large screen, serving as a portal to virtual worlds.
subjects: on justifying the hypothetical nature of art and the non-identicality within the object world

name: A-Volve by Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau
desc: A-Volve (1993–94) was an interactive-evolutionary art environment that stands as an important step in the development of AI art.

name: Second Reality Demo Released by Future Crew at Assembly 93
desc: At Assembly 93 in July 1993, Future Crew debuted Second Reality, a significant demo showcasing cutting-edge 2D and 3D computer graphics rendering.

name: Just This Once by Scott French
desc: Just This Once is a computer-generative romance novel authored by a Macintosh IIcx computer named “Hal” in collaboration with programmer Scott French.

name: “Computer Art” No More
desc: According to Art Historian Frank Popper, by 1993, the term “computer art” had evolved from a distinct category to simply one of many electronic art forms.

name: Virtual Reality: An Emerging Medium, held at the Guggenheim Museum
desc: The early ‘90s fascination with virtual reality continued with an exhibition at none other than the Guggenheim. The Guggenheim Museum’s Virtual Reality: An Emerging Medium was an Intel Digital Education & Arts Program event.

name: The world’s first smartphone
desc: The IBM Simon Personal Communicator, a handheld mobile device with a touchscreen is often hailed as the first true smartphone, making its debut in the United States.

name: Placeholder by Brenda Laurel and Rachel Strickland
desc: Another work of Virtual Reality in the early ‘90s, Placeholder, a VR initiative by Interval Research Corporation and The Banff Centre for The Performing Arts, was created by Brenda Laurel and Rachel Strickland.
subjects: placeholder: landscape and narrative in virtual environments

name: Genetic Images by Karl Sims
desc: Genetic Images, a groundbreaking media installation conceived by Karl Sims in 1993, explored the concept of interactive evolution within virtual environments.

name: Information Landscapes by Muriel Cooper
desc: Muriel Cooper’s Information Landscapes Project, made with David Small and six others, featured in MoMA’s collection and [unveiled at a 1994 TED talk, represented a pinnacle in her illustrious career](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BhrZHkdc2rU&ab_channel=MITMediaLab).

name: Galapagos by Karl Sims
desc: Karl Sims continued to pioneer evolutionary art with his work Galápagos, blending audience interaction with computational evolution.

name: Roman Verostko and Jean-Pierre Hébert
desc: Roman Verostko and Jean-Pierre Hébert founded “The Algorists,” along with Charles Csuri, Manfred Mohr, Mark Wilson and Ken Musgrave, to form a group based on the mutual adoration of the art that could be produced by algorithms.

name: unendlich, fast… by Holger Friese
desc: Another example of early net art, Holger Friese’s Unendlich, fast... was a bold departure from the early internet landscape, which emphasized clarity and navigability.

name: jodi.org by JODI
desc: In the early days of the public web, JODI emerged as pioneers of net art with their enigmatic website, begun around 1993, archived at [wwwwwwwww.jodi.org](https://wwwwwwwww.jodi.org/).

name: The Slade Centre for Electronic Media in Fine Art (SCEMFA) Opens
desc: The Slade Centre for Electronic Media in Fine Art (SCEMFA) was opened. The history of the department extends back to 1973 when Malcolm Hughes founded the Experimental Department at the Slade.
subjects: slade centre for electronic media in fine art (scemfa)

name: Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii by Nam June Paik
desc: Nam June Paik’s Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii captured the United States’ shift into the information age in the mid-90s with the uncertainty and optimism that entailed.

name: Google is born
desc: Larry Page and Sergey Brin met at Stanford in 1995 and formed their partnership the following year, when they built the search engine they called BackRub, running on Stanford’s servers.

name: Osmose by Char Davies
desc: Another early work of virtual reality and interactive art that anticipated virtual worlds, Char Davies’s Osmose transported participants into a perception distorting realm.

name: Puppet Motel by Laurie Anderson
desc: This “really significant work” in the rise of digital mass media art according to Casey Reas, Puppet Motel is an enigmatic CD-ROM by Laurie Anderson, designed with Hsin-Chien Huang and released on Voyager.

name: Rhizome Begins
desc: Rhizome begins: “Rhizome is the home of born-digital art and culture since 1996.” That 1996 start occurred when Mark Tribe founded Rhizome, initially as an email list that attracted some of the earliest artists exploring online mediums.

name: John Maeda joins the MIT Media Lab
desc: John Maeda’s arrival at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1996 marked a pivotal moment in the intersection of technology, design and art.

name: Sun Microsystems Release Java 1.0
desc: Despite initiating the project in June 1991, on January 23, 1996, JavaSoft, the newly formed operating company of Sun Microsystems, released Java 1.0, marking a significant milestone in the history of software development.

name: Macromedia Flash 1.0 Released
desc: December 19, 1996 marked the initial release of Macromedia Flash, a technology that paved the way rich graphics on the maturing web and for contemporary generative-web-based practices, pioneered by artists such as Joshua Davis, Yugo Nakamura, Brendan Dawes, James Paterson and LIA.

name: My boyfriend came back from the war Olia Lialina
desc: Another important example in the rise of Mass Media art, a Casey Reas precondition for NFTs, and net art, My boyfriend came back from the war by Olia Lialina is one of the most recognizable net art works.
subjects: my boyfriend came back from the war

name: Traffic, CAPC Musée d’Art Contemporain, Bordeaux
desc: With Traffic at Bordeaux’s CAPC Contemporary Museum, Nicolas Bourriaud introduced his concept of 'relational aesthetics,' art that [serves](https://formerwest.org/ResearchLibrary/Traffic) as “a vehicle for creating encounters between the artist and the viewers, the latter of which is ideally involved as an active participant.” The exhibition matters for this timeline because it stands as an example of the digital’s concerns manifested in the mainstream art world.

name: The Crossing by Bill Viola
desc: The Crossing by Bill Viola showcases his pioneering use of video technologies since the 1970s.

name: Form Art by Alexei Shulgin
desc: Alexei Shulgin’s Form Art is https://www.c3.hu/collection/form/index.html? of net art that explores the HTML language’s potential as a medium for artistic expression.

name: My Private Album by Feng Mengbo
desc: Feng Mengbo’s My Private Album was a pioneering work of interactive CD-ROM art, examining the combination of digital storytelling and interactivity.

name: World Skin by Maurice Benayoun
desc: This immersive art project used the CAVE, developed by Carolina Cruz-Neira, Daniel J. Sandin and Thomas A. DeFanti at the Electronic Visualization Laboratory, University of Illinois at Chicago.

name: ACU Program Begins
desc: According to Tom White, ACU, a key predecessor of Processing formed in 1998.

name: Frankensteinian Methods for Evolutionary Music Composition by Peter Todd and Gregory Werner
desc: This [book](https://direct.mit.edu/books/edited-volume/3910/chapter-abstract/164029/Frankensteinian-Methods-for-Evolutionary-Music?redirectedFrom=fulltext) chapter, “Frankensteinian Methods for Evolutionary Music Composition,” by Peter Todd and Gregory Werner looks at co-evolutionary techniques in music composition.
subjects: frankensteinian methods for evolutionary music composition

name: MPEG-4 standard announced
desc: An important step in the rise of Mass Media Art, an important pre-condition for NFTs, according to Casey Reas, in October 1998, the MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) announced the MPEG-4 standard, ISO/IEC 14496, following the success of MPEG-1 and MPEG-2.

name: Joshua Davis releases ps0.praystation.v0
desc: Flash creative coder pioneer Joshua Davis released ps0.praystation.v0, his website for exhibiting experimental design and art using code, specifically Flash.

name: Cities on the move: Contemporary Asian Art at the turn of the 21st c., Vienna
desc: Cities on the Move: Contemporary Asian Art at the Turn of the 21st Century” in Vienna, Austria, was the first presentation of a traveling exhibition curated by Hans Ulrich Obrist and Hou Hanru.

name: Inaugural International Generative Art Conference at Politecnico di Milano University
desc: For the purposes of this [Timeline](https://timeline.lerandom.art/), this event stands as tremendously more important than perhaps it should on first glance, as it marks the transition to the usage of the term of “generative art” as we understand and use it today.

name: SHREDDER by Mark Napier
desc: A classic of net. art, SHREDDER was a challenge to traditional print metaphors, embracing the web’s digita, data-based nature.

name: _readme – own, be owned, or remain invisible by Heath Bunting
desc: This pioneering work of net.art transforms a newspaper article about Heath Bunting, the artist, into a hyperlinked guide, where each word links to a corresponding website.

name: John Maeda publishes Design By Numbers
desc: In surely one of generative art’s most legendary moments, John Maeda published Design By Numbers, with the aim of simplifying programming for artists and designers at the MIT Media Lab’s Aesthetics and Computation Group.

name: Raging Bull and Deep ASCII by Vuk Cosic
desc: Based on custom software he developed in 1996 and released in 1998, according to DAM, Ćosić’s Raging Bull and Deep ASCII were some of the first ASCII films, as all the visuals are reduced to green ASCII characters.

name: Term Web 2.0 Coined by Darcy DiNucci
desc: Firmly in what many believe is the Web3 era, this nomenclature was first developed over twenty years prior. Darcy DiNucci coined the term “Web 2.0” in her article “Fragmented Future” for Print magazine.

name: Re-move by LIA
desc: Another important example of net.art and the rise of Mass Media art that was popularizing around the end of the decade, LIA’s Re-move (1999–2003) explores generative-audiovisual compositions that [combine](https://anthology.rhizome.org/re-move) organic forms “with the rawness of fin-de-siècle Viennese abstraction.” These works were originally created in Macromedia Director and released “on the internet to be accessible by everyone,” the artist told author Peter Bauman.

name: Stroud Cornock and Ernest Edmonds Meet in Leicester
desc: Leicester-based artists Stroud Cornock and Ernest Edmonds, working at Leicester School of Art and Leicester Technical College, recognize the potential of interactive computer-based art.

name: Leicester Polytechnic Is Formed
desc: Leicester Polytechnic is designated in April 1969, formed by the merger of Leicester School of Art and Leicester Technical College.

name: Ernest Edmonds Founds HCIRU Research Group
desc: Edmonds founded the Human Computer Interface Research Unit (HCIRU) at Leicester Polytechnic.

name: Ernest Edmonds Establishes LUTCHI Research Centre
desc: Edmonds moved from Leicester Polytechnic to Loughborough, establishing the Loughborough University of Technology Computer Human Interaction (LUTCHI) Research Centre.

name: Leicester Polytechnic officially Becomes De Montfort University
desc: As Leicester Polytechnic evolved into De Montfort University, its legacy as the epicenter for British (if not the world) computer art in the ‘70s and ‘80s remains.

name: Shoe-Field by Sonya Rapopport
desc: Shoe-Field (1982–89), an interactive artwork begun with a performance in a Berkeley computer store, offered a unique exploration of personal feelings about footwear.

name: Enter Y2K
desc: The decade of the 2000s began with the optimism of the dot-com era and the promise of the Internet’s potential.

name: Data Dynamics at the Whitney
desc: Curated by Christiane Paul and indicative of the early millennium enthusiasm for digital art—as the Internet sucked more and more of the cultural air—New York’s Whitney Museum hosted two major digital themed exhibitions in 2001 with Data Dynamics (March 2001) and BitStreams.

name: Digital Art by Christiane Paul
desc: This seminal book gave legitimacy to a field that was receiving renewed interest due to the success and rise of the Internet and net art.

name: Scott Draves developed the Fractal Flame algorithm
desc: Described by Arthur I.

name: Merkle Trees Added to Blockchain
desc: Stuart Haber, W. Scott Stornetta and Dave Bayer introduced Merkle trees, for which Ralph Merkle filed a patent in 1979, granted in 1982, to blockchain technology.

name: MPEG Established
desc: Dr. Hiroshi Yasuda and Dr. Leonardo Chiariglione founded MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group), which would go on to develop the MPEG standard, which is still largely in use to this day.

name: David Bowie and Ty Roberts Develop The Verbasizer
desc: [The Verbasizer](https://www.vice.com/en/article/xygxpn/the-verbasizer-was-david-bowies-1995-lyric-writing-mac-app) is developed by David Bowie and Ty Roberts as a way to automate and speed up Bowie’s long-standing technique of cutting up fragments of text and rearranging them at random to create song lyrics.

name: Vera Molnár Joins François at the Sorbonne
desc: Vera Molnár was heavily involved with Sorbonne University throughout the 1980s. In 1980, she and Franćois established the Centre de Recherche Expérimentale et Informatique des Arts Visuels (CREIAV).
subjects: centre de recherche expérimentale et informatique des arts visuels (creiav)
sorbonne department of plastic arts and art sciences

name: First do it Exhibition Takes Place
desc: This open exhibition premiered in 1994 at the Ritter Kunsthalle in Klagenfurt after its conceptual roots were laid the previous year.

name: do it Concept and Catalogue Released
desc: All about instruction-based generative art, do it began in 1993 as a conversation and a book of instructions from twelve artists, from which the exhibitions grew.

name: Stephen Todd Works on Early Computer Art
desc: Todd shared some of his early computer work with us recently, stating: “I suddenly remembered a bit of algorithmic 'art' from earlier: 1967. Modern day version https://jsfiddle.net/sjpt/x7qn9wgb/156/.

name: Calculated Movements by Larry Cuba
desc: In this masterpiece of computer animation, Calculated Movements, Larry Cuba demonstrates his painstaking method of computer animation, creating elaborately choreographed scenes using basic elements that are repeated and arranged in a hierarchical fashion.

name: Mark Wilson Publishes Drawing with Computers
desc: In what may be [the first creative coding book for artists, Mark Wilson published the seminal](http://mgwilson.com/Drawing%20with%20Computers.pdf) [Drawing with Computers](http://mgwilson.com/Drawing%20with%20Computers.pdf).

name: Eden by Jon McCormack
desc: Eden is an interactive, self-generating, artificial ecosystem installation active from 2004–2012.

name: Genomic Cartography: Chromosome 18, Ben Fry
desc: Part of MoMA’s permanent collection and from Fry‘s time at the MIT Media Lab’s Aesthetics and Computation Group, Chromosome 18 was part of genomic cartography and an example of Fry’s expert use and interest in data visualization.

name: Transmediale 2001: DIY (do it yourself!)
desc: Transmediale, the Berlin festival-conference, was emblematic of the excitement globally for software and net-based art at the turn of the new millennium, as in 2001 it introduced an artistic software award.

name: teamLab Formed
desc: Toshiyuki Inoko founded the digital art collective teamLab in 2001 with four friends, bringing together approximately 400 'ultratechnologists' with backgrounds across art, mathematics and technology.

name: Derivative launches TouchDesigner
desc: TouchDesigner, introduced by Derivative, marked a transformative advancement in interactive, real-time multimedia programming for visual artists.

name: Golan Levin and Casey Reas, The Art of Code at Bitforms, New York
desc: This exhibition featured Casey Reas’s Tissue, a continuation of Path from the year prior, which today is known as Phototaxis and can be found on Art Blocks. Levin exhibited his interactive work Meshy (1998).

name: Velvet Strike modifies Counter Strike
desc: In another classic work of video game history, Velvet-Strike, by Anne-Marie Schleiner, Joan Leandre and Brody Condon, merged activism with video-game art as it was a protest against the newly launched Bush-era war on terrorism.

name: Super Mario Clouds by Cory Arcangel
desc: In a masterpiece of video game art, Cory Arcangel deconstructs a familiar cultural artifact, reducing the iconic Super Mario Brothers game to its ethereal background only.

name: isometricblocks, Ben Fry
desc: Emanating from his tenure at the MIT Media Lab’s Aesthetics + Computation Group (ACG), Ben Fry’s isometricblocks (2002–2004) is a seminal work that marries generative art with genetic data visualization.

name: The first Processing Forum
desc: Generative art witnessed a significant community milestone with the launch of the Processing Forum, an online platform named [Discourse](https://discourse.processing.org/).

name: Samorost by Amanita Design
desc: This Flash art video game, known for its artistic emphasis, was created by Amanita Design, a Czech indie game studio.

name: Yugo Nakamura Launches yugop.com
desc: The Flash 4 savant Nakamura originally launched http://yugop.com in 1999. The Flash-based site demonstrated a masterful blend of simplicity and interactivity that would influence the trajectory of art and design on the web.

name: Substrate, Jared Tarbell
desc: Made with Processing, this 2003 masterpiece by Tarbell highlights one of the powers of generative art and computation: the ability to convey complexity from simplicity.

name: Twenty-Six Visions of Hildegarde by Roman Verostko
desc: Twenty-Six Visions of Hildegarde by Roman Verostko the pioneering Algorist who was deeply influenced by early twentieth-century abstractionists, was created for the SIGGRAPH 2004 Synaesthesia exhibition.

name: Reas Begins Process Series (2004-2010)
desc: In his seminal series Process, documented comprehensively in the book Process Compendium 2004-2010, Casey Reas explores the intricate phenomenon of emergence through his unique artistic system.

name: Cinema Redux, Brendan Dawes
desc: Part of MoMA’s permanent collection, Dawes’s Cinema Redux transformed the experience of a film into a singular visual artifact.

name: Matthew Cook proved that CA Rule 110 is capable of universal computation
desc: Matthew Cook’s proof, developed while assisting Stephen Wolfram on A New Kind of Science and published in Complex Systems in 2004, resolved a conjecture Wolfram had posited in the 1980s.

name: Margot Lovejoy Publishes Digital Currents: Art in the Electronic Age
desc: Similar To Christiane Paul’s Digital Art, Lovejoy’s book offers an insightful look into the transformative role of digital technologies in contemporary art.
subjects: digital currents: art in the electronic age

name: “New Masters of Flash” published by friends of ED
desc: While Flash was a tool bred from the 1990s, it still continued to be extensively used throughout this decade.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: {Software} Structures by Casey Reas, Jared Tarbell, Robert Hodgin and William Ngan
desc: This online commission for the Whitney Museum’s Artport was created by Casey Reas as a way to explain generative art’s ability to visualize the same simple instructions in many different ways depending on the execution of the artist’s algorithm.

name: Pac-Manhattan
desc: This IRL Pac-Man Pac-Manhattan was an innovative work of urban-performance art that transformed the streets of New York City into a live-action videogame, replicating the classic 1980's arcade game Pac-Man.

name: Facebook launches at Harvard
desc: On 4 February 2004 Mark Zuckerberg launched thefacebook.com, open at first only to Harvard e-mail addresses, marking a turning point in humanity’s relationship with communities and popularizing online identities and interactions in a way that mainstreamed what before was looked on as niche.

name: Pitch and Volume by Anna Ursyn
desc: Exhibited at SIGGRAPH 2004’s Synaesthesia, Pitch and Volume by Anna Ursyn, scrutinizes the intricate relationship between the digital and natural orders, exploring how both domains manifest structured patterns that can be perceived and analyzed.

name: Zach Lieberman releases OpenFrameworks v0.01
desc: With a decade titled the “Tooling Era,” tools clearly played a critical role in this decade’s impact on the history of generative thinking and art.

name: “Evolution and Collective Intelligence of the Electric Sheep” by Scott Draves
desc: This article, released in the book The Art of Artificial Evolution, showcases Draves’s innovative use of distributed computing via a screensaver that animates and evolves fractal art, the Electric Sheep that Draves began in 1999.
subjects: evolution and collective intelligence of the electric sheep

name: Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau’s Life Writer
desc: Christa Sommerer and Laurent Mignonneau’s Life Writer, an excellent example of mid-2000s cybernetic—or feedback loop-based art—that was artificial life in nature.

name: Machado and Cardoso’s NEvAr system
desc: Machado and Cardoso’s NEvAr system is an artistic tool that leverages concepts from evolutionary art.

name: Seven Easy Pieces by Marina Abramović at the Guggenheim
desc: In November 2005, Marina Abramović presented Seven Easy Pieces at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York.
subjects: how to explain pictures to a dead hare

name: Part Object Part Sculpture, Columbus, Ohio
desc: At Columbus, Ohio’s Wexner Center for the Arts, Part Object Part Sculpture, organized by curator Helen Molesworth, presented a compelling rethinking of post-World War II sculpture that highlighted the work of Duchamp’s Conceptualism in the art historical canon.

name: Desire of Codes, Seiko Mikami
desc: Seiko Mikami’s interactive installation Desire of Codes premiered at the Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM), critically merging human sensory perceptions with digital surveillance technology to reflect on the pervasive encoding in an information-oriented society.
subjects: yamaguchi center for arts and media (ycam)

name: Google Buys YouTube
desc: YouTube was created by three former PayPal employees and bought by Google, announced 9 October and completed 13 November 2006, for $1.65 billion in what some have described as “[the best tech deal ever.](https://www.theringer.com/2016/10/10/16042354/google-youtube-acquisition-10-years-tech-deals-69fdbe1c8a06)” The move signifies for the sake of this timeline, both the peak of Web2’s dominance and the ever-continuing rise of mass-media art.

name: Tumblr Launched
desc: Launched on 1 March 2007, Tumblr, founded by David Karp with lead developer Marco Arment, served as a critical place for the presentation and distribution of digital art from the mid- to late-2000s.

name: Steve Jobs Announces the iPhone
desc: On January 9, 2007, Steve Jobs changed the world by announcing the iPhone.

name: VVEBCAM by Petra Cortright
desc: The important work of software-badsed art was recorded on webcam by Post-Internet artist Petra Cortright is in the collection of MoMA, where it was [part of the 2020 gallery of the collection, “Search Engines.”](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/401436?installation_image_index=0) This seminal digital artwork explores the interface of self-presentation and digital manipulation.

name: RMB City by Cao Fei
desc: In the most well-known proto-Metaverse work, conceived by artist Cao Fei in the virtual world of Second Life, RMB City was a vibrant exploration of urban and cultural evolution within a fictional online Chinese metropolis.

name: All Streets by Ben Fry
desc: Perhaps Fry’s most well-known work and a standout work of data visualization, All Streets is a compelling visual representation of every road in the lower 48 states of the United States, totaling over 26 million individual road segments.

name: Wack! Art and the Feminist Revolution, Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles
desc: Organized by MOCA Curator Connie Butler, this was the first major museum exhibition to comprehensively examine the global impact and legacy of feminist art from 1965 to 1980.
subjects: wack! art and the feminist revolution

name: Atom by Christopher Bauder and Robert Henke
desc: This large-scale audio-visual experience by Christopher Bauder and Robert Henke used algorithmic choreography to transform a room into a dynamic, immersive environment.

name: Satoshi Nakamoto publishes Bitcoin Whitepaper
desc: Satoshi Nakamoto’s https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf is important to the story of digital art as it was the first conceptualization of a decentralized blockchain.

name: Casey Reas and Ben Fry Publish Processing Textbook
desc: In order to [lay out](https://medium.com/processing-foundation/a-modern-prometheus-59aed94abe85) “our vision for how Processing could be used in a university classroom,” Casey Reas and Ben Fry published the Processing textbook, Processing: a programming handbook for visual designers and artists.

name: Cory Arcangel Begins His Photoshop Gradients
desc: Cory Arcangel’s Photoshop Gradient and Smudge Tool Demonstration would go on to become some of the most well known software-based work of the decade.
subjects: photoshop gradient and smudge tool demonstration

name: Rondo by Anna Ursyn
desc: This work of digital generative art remains fascinating—a work so contemporary yet rooted in Fortran, a programming language dating to the 1950s.

name: Daito MANABE launches Rhizomatiks
desc: Rhizomatiks, a pioneering collective, emerged in 2006 and was renamed Abstract Engine in 2020, incorporated technology and artistry to focus on experimental projects that blended R&D with artistic expression.

name: 20th Century Computer Art at Tama Art University Museum, Tokyo
desc: The rise of educational tooling for artists in the first half of the decade, as we have covered, such as Processing and openFrameworks served the main purpose of making it easier for artists to create works using software.
subjects: 20th century computer art: beginnings and developments

name: 16 Études sur les origines de Blum by Vera Molnár
desc: The [grande dame herself, Vera Molnár](https://www.lerandom.art/editorial/molnars-paris), ventured into the literary domain with an unlikely commissioned tribute to James Joyce’s Ulysses.
subjects: 16 études sur les origines de blum

name: Deep Time of the Media: Toward an Archaeology of Hearing and Seeing by Technical Means by Siegfried Zielinski
desc: This book, first published in German in 2002 and a great influence on this very timeline, looks at sciences, technology and the arts from a deeply intellectually rigorous perspective, where Zielinski incorporates both historiography and philosophy to explore media’s archaeological depth.

name: Academy by R. Luke DuBois
desc: As included in Casey Reas’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA as a standout example of computer film, specifically digital video, Academy compresses seventy years of film history into the length of a seventy-six-minute film.
subjects: academy of motion picture arts and sciences

name: Twitter Founded
desc: Launched in the summer of 2006, just two years after the initial release of Facebook’s rising popularity, 2006 served as a critical year in the development of the social media-dominated period that would follow and in which we still largely live nearly twenty years later.

name: Monster Movie by Takeshi Murata
desc: In the collection of SFMOMA and included in Casey Reas’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA, Takeshi Murata’s sub-four-minute digital video, Monster Movie was a revolutionary work in digital video art.

name: scoreLight by Alvaro Cassinelli, Masatoshi Ishikawa, Yusaku Kuribara and Daito Manabe
desc: The innovative work from Japan explored the intersection of visual art and sound by transforming doodles and three-dimensional objects into musical sequences.

name: Len Sassaman ASCII Tribute on Bitcoin
desc: Mined on July 30 as part of Bitcoin Block 138725, this work stands as some of the earliest on-chain art and it is ASCII. The work itself is a tribute to Leonard “Len” Harris Sassaman.

name: Bitcoin Genesis Block
desc: The Bitcoin genesis block executed by Satoshi Nakamoto demonstrated the workability of Bitcoin as more than just a concept.

name: Processos criativos com os meios eletrônicos: poéticas digitais
desc: This book taught a generation of Brazilian creative coders in the mid-to-late ‘90s. The book investigated the technical mechanisms behind electronic image creation.
subjects: processos criativos com os meios eletrônicos: poéticas digitais

name: Documenta Done by the net art pioneer Vuk Ćosić
desc: Documenta Done by the net art pioneer Vuk Ćosić subverts institutional control over net art’s circulation, epitomizing the artist’s role as a digital pirate.

name: Legend of the net.art coinage
desc: There is https://www.artforum.com/features/web-work-a-history-of-internet-art-2-162477/ that has persisted—https://rhizome.org/editorial/2017/jan/12/a-net-artist-named-google-1/—that net.art was first coined by Vuk Ćosić from a garbled email.

name: Spiral 5 PTL by Dan Sandin, Tom DeFanti and Mimi Shevitz
desc: This early computer graphics art video by Dan Sandin, Tom DeFanti and Mimi Shevitz uses the image processor as a musical instrument, generating variations on a spiral motif synchronized with an eclectic audio track.

name: Ray Kurzweil’s Cybernetic Poet
desc: [Ray Kurzweil’s Cybernetic Poet](https://www.kurzweilcyberart.com/poetry/rkcp_how_it_works.php) first written in the mid-1980s, creates language models of the works of various human authors and uses language analysis and mathematical modeling to generate original poems “inspired” by these authors.

name: Christian Bök Publishes “The Piecemeal Bard is Deconstructed”
desc: Writing in response to RACTER’s The Policeman’s Beard is Half-Constructed, Christian Bök publishes the essay “[The Piecemeal Bard is Deconstructed: Notes Toward a Poential Robopoetics,](https://www.ubu.com/papers/object/03_bok.pdf)” in [Object 10: Cyberpoetics](https://www.ubu.com/papers/object.html) (edited by Kenneth Goldsmith).

name: Allison Parrish Launches Everyword
desc: Allison Parrish launches [@everyword](https://twitter.com/everyword), a Twitter poetry bot tasked with tweeting “every word in the English language, in alphabetical order, one word at a time, every thirty minutes.” The bot completed its mission in June 2014.

name: Soft Cinema by Lev Manovich
desc: As included in Casey Reas’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA, Manovich’s Soft Cinema is an innovative exploration into the dynamics of digital cinema.

name: Agent Ruby by Lynn Hershman Leeson
desc: An important example in the development of AI art by Lesson, Agent Ruby (1998–2002), commissioned by SFMOMA, grew out of the expanded cinema experience from Leeson’s film Teknolust.

name: Fuse by Scott Draves
desc: This moment stands as one of the earliest predecessors of the big-data, machine-learning AI art of today, as opposed to the symbolic AI art of Harold Cohen.

name: Nettime Forms and net.art Begins
desc: In the spring of 1995, Nettime, a mailing list and platform that was instrumental in the formation of net.art, formed. The list gathered the earliest net.art practitioners and was where the term took hold.

name: skinonskinonskin by Auriea Harvey and Michaël Samyn
desc: This pioneering work of Flash art and net.art by Auriea Harvey and Michaël Samyn, skinonskinonskin, was a collection of the pair’s digital love letters.

name: Evolved Virtual Creatures by Karl Sims
desc: This is an early example of art built on artificial neural networks, although the networks were evolved by genetic algorithms rather than trained on data.

name: Waiting Room by Mark Napier
desc: Waiting Room by Mark Napier is an innovative exploration of digital space and collaborative art, engaging 50 online users in a shared creative experience that bridges the realms of net.art and proto-AI art.

name: Parallel 1 by Harun Farocki
desc: Included in Casey Reas’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA as a standout example of computer film, this 16-minute digital video explores the evolution of computer graphics within the larger four-part series Parallel, which examines the genre of computer animation.

name: Summer by Olia Lialina
desc: Included in Casey Reas’s course, 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA, is a standout example of net art and the only piece appearing outside the decade of the ‘90s.

name: MuirMcNeil founded
desc: Founded by Paul McNeil and Hamish Muir, MuirMcNeil uses software to explore parametric design systems in typography and graphic design. Their work can be seen as generative typography or generative design.

name: Marius Watz Begins generator.x Project
desc: In an important early attempt at digital preservation, Marius Watz began his generator.x project documenting generative art in collaboration with Atle Barcley, director of Atelier Nord.

name: Yellowtail by Golan Levin
desc: This now legendary piece of software was begun by Levin at the Interval Research Corporation in 1998 and completed at MIT in 1999 and 2000.

name: Gustave Courbet’s Pavilion of Realism
desc: In what Hans Ulrich Obrist considers the birth of Modernism, Gustave Courbet erected—at his own expense—the Pavilion of Realism in 1855, eight years prior to the Salon des Refusés.

name: Peacock Room by James Whistler
desc: James Whistler’s Peacock Room stands as an important example in the history of installation and immersive art, which has a rich tradition in digital art.
subjects: art and money; or, the story of the room

name: Spectacle, Speculation, Spam by Alan Warburton
desc: Included in Casey Reas’s course 50 Years of Software Artists at UCLA as a standout example of computer film, Alan Warburton’s digital video Spectacle, Speculation, Spam is a video essay he made for the Edge of Frame Weekend seminar at The Whitechapel Gallery in East London.

name: The Artist Is Present by Marina Abramovic at MoMA
desc: Marina Abramović creates analog, performance- and system-based work that elevates audience participation and the role of the viewer in the vein of interactive software art.

name: Mothership by Jonathan Monaghan
desc: This work is considered to be a prototype for contemporary NFTs, as it is one of the earliest digital artworks to use a blockchain as a decentralized ledger.

name: Written Images by Martin Fuchs and Peter Bichsel
desc: This book represents an attempt at a generative physical book, as each “programmed book” was a copy uniquely generated via digital printing.

name: Processing Foundation Begins
desc: Ben Fry, Casey Reas and Daniel Shiffman started the Processing Foundation—more than ten years after Processing’s initial release—to champion software literacy within the arts and artistic expression through technology, particularly for communities traditionally marginalized by the tech industry.

name: Re:MARK by Golan Levin & Zach Lieberman
desc: A commission of the Ars Electronica Museum of the Future, Re:MARK, by Tmema (Golan Levin and Zachary Lieberman) with production support from the Ars Electronica Futurelab, was an interactive installation that visualized speech as whimsical animated text and shapes.

name: Alphabet Synthesis Machine by Golan Levin
desc: The culmination of several years of collaboration between Golan Levin, Jonathan Feinberg, and Cassidy Curtis, Alphabet Synthesis Machine was an online interactive artwork commissioned by PBS and Art21.org.

name: First ART && CODE Conference Organized by Golan Levin
desc: Organized by Golan Levin to promote software-arts education, the conference took place from March 7-9, 2009, at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, focusing on “programming environments for artists, young people, and the rest of us.” It attracted 234 attendees from 7 countries and 23 U.S.

name: Cinder Launched
desc: Cinder is an open-source creative coding software tool developed by Andrew Bell and released to the public in 2010.

name: Three.js Released
desc: Three.js, a JavaScript library for creating 3D animations was initially released on April 24, 2010 by Ricardo Cabello, otherwise known as mrdoob.

name: iPad Announced
desc: If the previous decade saw the launch of “smart devices” and “social media 1.0” with Apple’s iPhone and Facebook, the 2010s saw revamped iterations of these phenomena almost immediately.

name: Instagram Launches
desc: Social medial 2.0 began in earnest with Instagram.

name: onformative Founded
desc: Founded by Julia Laub and Cedric Kiefer, onformative is a studio that focuses on digital generative art and design.

name: “Characteristics of pattern formation” by Jeff Jones
desc: Fully titled “Characteristics of pattern formation and evolution in approximations of Physarum transport networks,” this highly influential article would go on to inspire the work of both Sage Jenson and fxhash Founder Baptiste Crespy, ciphrd.

name: NONOTAK Formed
desc: Formed by Noemi Schipfer and Takami Nakamoto, NONOTAK merges the creative fields of visual arts and architecture with music.

name: Rafaël Rozendaal, Into Time with mirrors
desc: Taking a cue from net.art, Rozendaal uses the Internet as his canvas yet his work often conveys multiple materialities.

name: Manolo Begins Processing Sketches
desc: Manolo Gamboa Naon (aka Manoloide) began his Processing sketches in 2012, according to himself on [his github page](https://github.com/manoloide/AllSketchs).

name: Ghosts in the Machine at the New Museum, New York
desc: This exhibition examined the evolving reciprocity between humans, machines and art.
subjects: the machine as seen at the end of the mechanical age

name: Taeyoon Choi, Zach Lieberman, Jen Lowe and Amit Pitaru Co-Found the School for Poetic Computation (SFPC)
desc: After teaching for a decade at Parsons School of Design, where he also studied under Golan Levin, Zach Lieberman helped create the School for Poetic Computation in New York with Taeyoon Choi, Jen Lowe and Amit Pitaru.

name: Lauren Lee McCarthy Creates p5.js
desc: Lauren Lee McCarthy created p5.js roughly twelve years after the initial release of Processing in 2001.

name: Beautypi Starts ShaderToy
desc: In January, 2013, [Shadertoy.com](http://shadertoy.com/) was created by Pol Jeremias and [Inigo Quilez](https://iquilezles.org/) (Beautypi) as a repository for community-shared shaders.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Ascribe Conceptualizes Proto-NFTs
desc: Ascribe conceptualized the concept of owning digital art on a blockchain “like you own bitcoin” throughout 2013, finally launching publicly at the end of 2014.

name: BANK by Kevin Abosch
desc: BANK by Kevin Abosch is one of the earliest works by the mixed-media and AI artist. BANK is also one of the earliest artistic explorations of the blockchain.

name: Jerobeam Fenderson and Hansi3D Begin Oscilloscope Music
desc: Jerobeam Fenderson and Hansi3D started Oscilloscope Music, a project focusing on audiovisual oscilloscope explorations; the OsciStudio software followed in 2017. Reminiscent of Mary Ellen Bute, Ben Laposky and Herbert W.

name: “Ten Questions Concerning Generative Computer Art” by McCormack et al.
desc: In a text critical to both Philip Galanter’s and my own understanding of generative art, Jon McCormack and his colleagues examined the complexities and evolving nature of generative computer art in their article in the April 2014 issue of Leonardo.
subjects: ten questions concerning generative computer art

name: NILIcoin by Nili Lerner
desc: Lerner’s pre-community, proto-NFTS—along with work by the McCoys and Rhea Myers were, [according to Jason Bailey](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZY-VformTig), the “closest thing to early NFTs” as we now know them.

name: Is Art by Rhea Myers
desc: This piece from July 23, 2014, under three months after Quantum is another proto-NFT from 2014, yet it derives inspiration from Duchamp, 1960s Conceptualism and net.art.

name: Ian Goodfellow Introduces GANs
desc: In one of this story’s most relevant moments, Ian Goodfellow and his colleagues at the University of Montreal introduced the world to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), revolutionizing—and I don’t use the word lightly—the field of machine learning.

name: Art Post-Internet at UCCA, Beijing
desc: Curated by Karen Archey and Robin Peckham, this exhibition was an important look at the role of networked technology—the Internet—in contemporary art.

name: Kathleen and Arthur Breitman Propose Tezos
desc: Arthur Breitman, writing as L.M Goodman, released two Tezos papers in 2014 that proposed and described the Tezos blockchain for the first time.

name: Vitalik Buterin Publishes Ethereum Whitepaper
desc: Vitalik Buterin created Ethereum with the [Ethereum Whitepaper](https://ethereum.org/content/whitepaper/whitepaper-pdf/Ethereum_Whitepaper_-_Buterin_2014.pdf), marking a pivotal shift in the story of blockchains.

name: Rare Pepes by Joe Looney
desc: [According to Jason Bailey](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZY-VformTig), 2016 saw the introduction of the first community NFTs.

name: Factory of the Sun by Hito Steyerl at MOCA
desc: Premiering at the German Pavilion of the 2015 Venice Biennale before touring internationally, The Museum of Contemporary Art described the work as a “landmark video installation.” The piece was the talk of Venice at the time, with Google Arts & Culture describing it as “probably the most talked-about piece at the significant biennale.” Factory of the Sun blends the symbolism of sunlight with digital age critiques, employing a video game format to explore the paradox of the Internet’s utopian promise versus its oppressive transparency.

name: Zurich HB Flap by Andreas Gysin & Sidi Vanetti
desc: This generative-kinetic installation was the opening at exhibit at the new Museum of Digital Art (MuDA) Zurich, which began in 2016.

name: Zach Lieberman Begins Daily Instagram Animations
desc: Like Manolo and Takawo before him, Zach Lieberman began the practice of doing daily animations on Instagram in 2016.

name: A Companion to Digital Art by Christiane Paul
desc: In the follow-up companion to the seminal Digital Art, Paul’s A Companion to Digital Art offered a comprehensive exploration of digital art’s evolution, aesthetics and politics.

name: Electronic Superhighway (2016-1966) at Whitechapel Gallery, London
desc: This major exhibition of digital art featured over 100 works exploring the impact of computer and Internet technologies on art.

name: “So you want to build a generator” by Kate Compton
desc: Golan Levin considers this article, “[So you want to build a generator](https://www.tumblr.com/galaxykate0/139774965871/so-you-want-to-build-a-generator)” by Kate Compton, to be “foundational for generative art” along with Max Bense’s “Projects of Generative Aesthetics” (1965).
subjects: so you want to build a generator

name: Open Codes at ZKM Center for Art and Media
desc: Open Codes, described by Georg Bak to Le Random in our Twitter Spaces Launch as “the exhibition of our times,” was curated by the legendary Peter Weibel with Lívia Nolasco-Rózsás, Yasemin Keskintepe and Blanca Giménez.

name: Crystal Towers by Matt DesLauriers
desc: Crystal Towers by Matt DesLauriers is a data-driven generative algorithm created with Node.js, Three.js and Blender.

name: Curios Cards: First Art NFT on Ethereum
desc: With the 2017 rapid increase in cryptocurrency prices, or “bull run,” the first NFTs proper appeared. Predating CryptoPunks by just over a month, Curio Cards stand as the first-art NFT project on Ethereum.

name: Matt Hall and John Watkinson Release CryptoPunks
desc: The first large generative character set minted on Ethereum, CryptoPunks was released by Matt Hall and John Watkinson of Larva Labs on June 22, 2017 for free.

name: Creeps & Weirdos by DADA.nyc
desc: Aligned with previous NFT attempts by the McCoys and ascribe, DADA aimed to empower artists by enabling more people to earn a sustainable living as artists.
subjects: the blockchain art market is here

name: “The Blockchain Art Market Is Here” by Jason Bailey (Artnome)
desc: After purchasing a CryptoKitty during the 2017 crypto bull run, Jason Bailey (Artnome) wrote, “The Blockchain Art Market Is Here.” The piece articulates Bailey’s prescient conviction that blockchains and NFTs would eventually have a big impact on artists and the art market, writing that he “strongly suggest[s] artists and art collectors take blockchain seriously and monitor the market.” While this idea had been expressed by artists at least back to 2014 with Kevin McCoy, Jonathan Monaghan, Nili Learner, Rhea Myers, Kevin Abosch and others, it took the popularity of CryptoKitties and its headlining grabbing numbers to actually initiate a rapid increase in adoption.
subjects: the blockchain art market is here

name: CryptoKitties Launches
desc: One of the earliest NFT projects and blockchain games that reached mania status was CryptoKitties, launching in November 2017 in the midst of a parabolic rise in the price of cryptocurrencies.

name: Tezos ICO
desc: Tezos ICO-ed in July, 2017 with a “Proof-of-Stake” (PoS) consensus model, allowing token holders to stake—lock up their coins—to validate new blocks, for which they received additional tokens as a reward.

name: Chance and Control: Art in the Age of Computers at the V&A
desc: Another indication that institutional interest renewed during the first crypto market bull run, perhaps already with the hope that cryptocurrency interest could drive interest in digital art.
subjects: chance and control: art in the age of computers

name: Rare Digital Art Festival #1, New York
desc: With the idea of Joe Looney from Rare Pepe Wallet and organized by R.A.R.E, this milestone event in NFT history kicked off in January 2018 with a huge event in this story: RARE AF #1 NYC, the first Rare Art Festival.

name: R.A.R.E Art Labs Launched
desc: One of the earliest commercial NFT platforms, along with SuperRare, R.A.R.E (Rare Art Registry and Exchange) Art Labs was founded, introducing the R.A.R.E Protocol, one of the earliest crypto-economies for the digital art world.

name: SuperRare launches
desc: In April, SuperRare, one of the oldest surviving crypto art marketplaces, launched its beta smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain.

name: Christie’s First Art + Tech Summit
desc: Christie’s inaugurated its Art+Tech Summit at its London headquarters on July 18.

name: Dieter Shirley and Others Propose the ERC-721 Standard
desc: William Entriken, Dieter Shirley, Jacob Evans and Nastassia Sachs authored the ERC-721 protocol, proposed in January 2018 as Ethereum’s first NFT token standard, laying the foundation for the variety of ways NFTs remain used to this day.

name: Putting the Pieces Back Together Again by Ralf Baeker
desc: This autonomous kinetic installation explores self-organization and emergent complex behavior based on a reimagination of cybernetic art in the twenty-first century.
subjects: putting the pieces back together again

name: All We’d Ever Need Is One Another by Adam Basanta
desc: This mixed-media AI installation autonomously generates images, embodying a self-sustaining “art factory,” an early example of work employing material, coded and AI-generative techniques.
subjects: all we'd ever need is one another
coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Christie’s First Sale of an AI artwork
desc: This sale could in some ways be considered the initial spark that lit the fuse of the upcoming NFT craze, peaking in 2021.
subjects: automat und mensch: a history of ai and generative art

name: Chaos Machine by Distributed Gallery
desc: Chaos Machine demonstrates the breadth and materiality of blockchain-based generative art.

name: Tezos Mainnet Goes Live
desc: Despite legal action that delayed Tezos’s initial release by nearly a year, the chain officially launched on mainnet on September 17, 2018. The project was watched closely, as it had been one of the largest ICOs at the time.

name: Memories of Passersby I by Mario Klingemann
desc: While first exhibited in January 2019 at Madrid’s Colección SOLO, Memories of Passersby I is an AI artwork generating an endless stream of unique, real-time portraits.

name: uumwelt by Pierre Huyghe
desc: Pierre Huyghe’s exploration of early AI technology at the Serpentine Galleries involved a transformative and autonomous art installation based on MRI scans, live animals and intense audience interaction.

name: Programmed: Rules, Codes, and Choreographies in Art, 1965–2018 at The Whitney
desc: An indication, like in 2001, that institutions—forced apparently largely to be reactionary—are willing to show interest in digital art following a catalyst that sparks renewed public interest.

name: Meandering River by onformative
desc: This AI audiovisual installation explores the transformative forces of nature through real-time algorithmic visuals and AI-composed music.

name: First Contemporary and Digital Art Fair (CADAF) in New York
desc: May saw another legendary blockchain art event with the first annual Contemporary and Digital Art Fair (CADAF) in New York City.

name: Larva Labs Releases Autoglyphs
desc: A seminal event in generative art history stands as April’s release of Autoglyphs by Larva Labs.

name: Rare Digital Art Festival #2, New York
desc: Running until the summer of 2022, Rare AF was the original on-chain art event that paved the way for Bright Moments, Proof of People and the variety of other Web3 native art events that now dot the yearly social calendar.

name: Automat und Mensch at Kate Vass Galerie
desc: The exhibition Automat und Mensch: A History of AI and Generative Art in May 2019 anticipated the arrival of AI and generative art.
subjects: automat und mensch: a history of ai and generative art

name: MACHINE HALLUCINATION by Refik Anadol
desc: This large-scale immersive audiovisual installation marked Anadol’s first major installation in New York City, and extended the machine learning practice he had begun with Archive Dreaming in 2017.

name: The Art of Cybersecurity by Brendan Dawes
desc: This data art project that visualizes cybersecurity threat data as a series of algorithmically generated images and a 4K animation.

name: CODED FIELD by Rhizomatiks
desc: This large-scale Rhizomatiks installation and dance performance, with technical and creative direction by Daito Manabe and choreography by MIKIKO, was held at the Tokyo FESTIVAL.
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982

name: Harm van den Dorpel Opens Left Gallery
desc: Left Gallery—a visionary early nft-based playform, according to Casey Reas—was started by Harm van den Dorpel and Paloma Rodríguez Carrington.

name: Ethereum Officially Launches
desc: Around two years after the release of Vitalik Buterin’s Whitepaper, on July 30, 2015, Ethereum initiated its launch process with its genesis block. This release was known as “Frontier” and marked Ethereum’s experimental beginnings.

name: Google’s Alexander Mordvintsev Launches DeepDream
desc: 2015 stands as a monumental year in this story—up there with 1965 (digital art’s public beginnings) and 1995 (net.art)—as the year AI art properly took off.

name: Akihiro Kubota’s ARTSAT1:INVADER Launches Generative Art Satellite
desc: ARTSAT project, a collaboration between Tama Art University and The University of Tokyo, launched the world’s first art satellite, ARTSAT1: INVADER.

name: Shunsuke Takawo Begins his Daily Coding
desc: Takawo began his habit of daily creative coding using Processing in 2015. By 2019, he transitioned to p5.js, sharing his work on OpenProcessing under a Creative Commons license.

name: From the Archives: Art and Technology at LACMA, 1967–1971 at Los Angeles County Museum of Art
desc: From the Archives: Art and Technology at LACMA, 1967–1971 offered insights into the museums influential Art & Technology Program and exhibition, which was mentioned previously on this timeline (1971).
subjects: coded: art enters the computer age, 1952–1982
from the archives: art and technology at lacma, 1967–1971

name: Rare AF3 Goes Virtual
desc: Scheduled to be held in the middle of the pandemic, Rare Art Festival (RareAF) transitioned to a fully virtual experience, VRAF. The festival showcased a diverse range of art forms within platforms like Cryptovoxels.

name: Chromie Squiggle by Snowfro
desc: Years in the making, the Art Blocks genesis project’s first iterations appeared on Twitter in September 2018 over two years before its official release on November 27, 2020.

name: INTANGIBLE FORMS by Shohei Fujimoto
desc: This immersive, audiovisual exhibition was Fujimoto’s first solo show in North America, featuring over nine real-time, light-based installations powered by choreographed kinetic lasers, strobes, haze and moving lights.

name: Composition by teamLab
desc: This light sculpture on a flat plane above the viewer continued the two-decade career of the audio and light installation artists, teamLab, from Japan.

name: Noteworthy AI Work
desc: From about 2019, the amount of AI work increased exponentially.

name: Archetype by Kjetil Golid
desc: Released on February 27, Golid’s Archetype was another early 2021 project that would later assume legendary status after a relatively quiet release on Art Blocks Curated.

name: DALL-E Launched
desc: We open January 2021 with a bang. This consequential deep learning model designed by OpenAI “generates”—as in creates—digital images from natural language descriptions.

name: Sotheby’s Natively Digital Sale
desc: In June, Sotheby’s held its first-ever curated NFT auction, Natively Digital, marking a pivotal moment in the integration of digital art within the traditional art world.

name: Mark Cuban Enters NFTs
desc: While ultimately not a mainstream success, Cuban’s NFT viewing gallery, Lazy, demonstrated the Web3 and NFT world’s rapid rise in prominence, especially after the March Beeple sale.

name: Takawo Founds Japan Generative Art Foundation (JGAF)

desc: In its second-to-last stop on its global tour, Bright Moments brought its traveling community and immersive minting and art experience to NFT Paris, transforming a café into a hub for generative and AI-based art, organized by artist Emily Edelman.

name: The Best of Times
desc: 2024 was a big year. It’s so hard to tell living through it; it’s hard to hear clearly in the din of noise. It was also a year of contrasts. It was the best of times, it was—you know.

name: Lawrence Lek Wins 2024 Artist Award at Frieze London
desc: In October during Frieze London, it’s notable to point out that the fair’s main award went to an AI artist in 2024, Lawrence Lek.

name: Taschen Releases On NFTs by Robert Alice
desc: February 22nd in Paris marked the launch of Taschen’s On NFTs, an early major art historical survey of the NFT ecosystem, authored by artist and researcher Robert Alice.

name: PXL DEX by Kim Asendorf
desc: The end of January saw one of the year’s strongest projects right off the bat.

name: Infinite Images at Toledo Museum of Art
desc: July saw undoubtedly one of the year’s most significant events for digital art.

infinite images: the art of algorithms

name: DeepSeek Shocks AI World
desc: In late January, DeepSeek released its R1 reasoning model, built on December’s V3. These models shocked the world, as overnight and from seemingly out of nowhere, they matched ChatGPT’s latest benchmarks at a fraction of the price.

name: Digital Art Mile at Art Basel
desc: June’s impressive Digital Art Mile returned to Basel for a second year.

name: Cycles by Material Protocol Arts
desc: Another major protocolic art to start the year, Cycles by Material Protocol Arts is a generative artwork on Ethereum, a self-described network sculpture composed of space and time.

name: “AI Art” Has a Moment
desc: In the first quarter of 2025, AI art moved from a steady undercurrent to a full-on cultural flashpoint. After January’s DeepSeek shock, attention only accelerated when Christie’s staged a high-profile AI-focused sale.

name: Beeple’s Studio Shows
desc: Since March 2023, Beeple Studios in Charleston has developed an ongoing cadence of public-facing shows that treat his practice as a lab for participative experimentation.

name: NFC Lisbon
desc: In early June, the crypto-adjacent art world descended on Lisbon for its annual NFC organized by John Karp.

name: New York Scene Transforms
desc: 2025 saw New York’s grip as the epicenter of digital art tighten.

name: Zero 10 Debuts at Art Basel Miami Beach
desc: Zero 10 is a case study for our times. It’s clear that 2025–2026 is a transition period for (the world,) the art world and digital art.

name: Starmirror by Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst
desc: One of my works of the year and one that crystallizes many of my current thoughts about where art is headed (living protocol stacks that form worlds) is Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst’s Starmirror at KW Institute for Contemporary Art, which I discussed with the artists [here](https://www.lerandom.art/editorial/holly-herndon-mat-dryhurst-on-artificial-psychedelia).

name: Vibe Check: A Brave New World
desc: You can sum up 2025 in two words: vibe coding. There. Timeline 2025 finished. But wait. That’s not all.
subjects: infinite images: the art of algorithms

name: Major New Digital Spaces Announced in Canyon, NODE and SOLO CSV
desc: If anything defined 2025 besides vibe coding, it was change. Institutions were responding to how art itself is changing, becoming more dynamic, interactive, world-like, living, intelligent.

name: Machine Love at Mori Art Museum
desc: One of the year’s major digital institutional shows, Machine Love at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum framed the post-pandemic acceleration of AI and virtual life as both medium and subject.
subjects: machine love: video game, ai and contemporary art

name: The World Through AI at Jeu de Paume
desc: Another of the year’s major institutional surveys of AI-driven art, The World Through AI at Paris’s Jeu de Paume, framed artificial intelligence as a split field.

name: Standouts of 2025
desc: Below is my standout art (shows and works) of 2025. In some special cases, they are written about as standalone moments as well. 1. Claude Opus 4.5 2. Room Service at Glitch Residency 3. Basel Social Club, Bank 4.
subjects: compositions in code: the art of processing and p5.js
the great adventure of material world

name: Basel Social Club’s Bank
desc: Also at Basel and easily, easily, easily one of my favorite shows of the year, the most fun, one of the most exciting and with the most durable residence in my head still.

name: AI and Creativity at Conferences
desc: With CVPR and NeurIPS, the world’s two most important annual AI conferences, creativity continued to be spotlighted.

name: Drifella III by Evil Biscuit
desc: If 2025 marked wider acceptance of the avant NFT scene, its culminating statement was Drifella III, Evil Biscuit’s hyper-“schizocollage” project. The work was some of the strongest of the year, to me.

name: Sasha Stiles at MoMA
desc: This show and New York’s Museum of Modern Art’s continued support for the digital with their lobby garden screen demonstrate institutional adoption of digital culture at the highest level.

name: Web3 Wind Downs
desc: Late January and early February 2026 really felt like the end. If Beeple’s $69 million sale on Nifty Gateway kicked off the NFT craze around five years prior, what did is closing signify?

name: One Of Us Is Real And It’s Not You at Galerie Yeche Lange
desc: Speaking of exciting New York digital-friendly galleries, hello, Galerie Yeche Lange.
subjects: one of us is real and it's not you

name: Frieder Nake Wins 2025 ACM SIGGRAPH Distinguished Artist Award for Lifetime Achievement in Digital Art
desc: Frieder Nake received the 2025 ACM SIGGRAPH Distinguished Artists Award for Lifetime Achievement in Digital Art, recognizing his foundational role in early computer and algorithmic art in addition to his long influence on computer graphics and digital art.

name: Autonomous Forest by terra0
desc: “A living work of art,” Autonomous Forest frames ecological stewardship as a techno-legal artwork.

name: Show of the year: Glitch’s Room Service
desc: The show of the year for me was Room Service, Glitch Residency’s collaborative, sprawling, relational, all-night culmination in a Burgundy chateau.

name: Art of the Year: Claude Opus 4.5
desc: If nothing dominated 2025 like vibe coding, then the art of the year should be…Claude Opus 4.5.

name: Karpathy Coins “Vibe Coding”
desc: In early February 2025, [Andrej Karpathy coined the term “vibe coding” in a tweet](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383?s=20).
